Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can help reduce the impact of bias in training machine learning models for predicting cell morphology. However, existing methods of representing cell shapes face certain limitations: voxel-based approaches are inefficient due to the storage requirements of a large number of voxels, and polygon meshes may not accurately represent cells with intricate, non-manifold geometries. To address these issues, we propose representing cell shapes as level sets of signed distance functions, which can capture complex cell membrane structures and provide a more efficient and accurate representation compared to voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches. To create a practical synthetic cell shape model, we developed a new method that involves defining a base cell shape and randomly generating distance field offsets based on a Gaussian distribution. To break up repeated patterns, we introduced a variant that combines the efficiency of level sets with the ability to create cell shapes with unique details. We evaluated our method by using it to learn a segmentation model that predicted cell membrane regions from fluorescent microscopy images with artificially introduced variations in cell shape. The results showed that the model was able to adapt to the shape changes and accurately identify the cell membrane in each image. The efficiency of level sets also enabled the training of a model that could handle a large number of synthetic cell shapes. To make this approach more accessible, we provided an open-source implementation of the synthetic cell shape generator. The implementation includes a user-friendly interface that allows for the definition of cell shapes with different structures, and automatically generates a distance field representation of the shape for use in training machine learning models. The synthetic cell shape generator can be used to predict cell membrane segments in images of various cell shapes and can be found at the following repository URL: https://github.com/lyc-ucsb/synthetic-cell-shapes. Additionally, a video showcasing the synthetic cell shapes and a sample model's predictions can be found at the following URL: https://www.lyc-ucsb.com/synthetic-cell-shapes/. To ensure reproducibility, the details of the model used in the study, including its training parameters, can be found in the repository at the following URL: https://github.com/lyc-ucsb/synthetic-cell-shapes. The synthetic cell shape approach can be used to represent a wide range of geometric cell types and can significantly reduce the impact of bias in training segmentation models, as shown by our experiments with a PECAM-positive cell type. The results of the study demonstrate the effectiveness of the level sets of signed distance functions in representing cell shapes and generating synthetic cell shapes with unique details.

import numpy as np

def calculate_autocorrelation(polarization, steps, time, show_plot=False):
    # Compute autocorrelation
    correlation = np.correlate(polarization, polarization, mode='full')[::steps][-len(polarization):]
    correlation /= np.mean(polarization**2)
    # Show plot if requested
    if show_plot:
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
        plt.plot(correlation)
        plt.xlabel('Time step')
        plt.ylabel('Autocorrelation')
        plt.show()
    return correlation

# Example usage
steps = int(1e4)
time = int(1e3)
polarization = np.random.normal(0.5, 0.05, steps)
calculate_autocorrelation(polarization, steps, time, show_plot=True)

Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach surpasses baseline results, significantly reducing Error Rates and increasing F-scores for location-aware detection. The traditional approach focuses on the maxima of spectrogram peaks. Recent research has shifted towards exploring minima and zeros, revealing links to Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). Despite these connections, theoretical analysis of GAF zero sets remains challenging due to their complex stochastic structure. Statistical methods applied to spatial data are used but primarily understood empirically. This work explores the geometric stochastic properties of spectrogram level sets, providing rigorous theorems that underpin spectrogram-based denoising techniques for time-series data. These findings are utilized to develop a rigorous method for spectrogram-based denoising, offering a theoretical framework that complements empirical approaches. Based on these insights, a novel algorithm is introduced for spectrogram-based signal denoising. Various experimental results are presented, demonstrating that this method is effective at removing noise from noisy time-series data. The stability of spectrogram levels and levels from GAFs is also empirically analyzed over different periods of time. The studies conducted show that these stochastic geometries exhibit marked differences. Additionally, a relationship between spectrogram levels and levels from GAFs is confirmed through empirical studies, demonstrating that both share a connection with Gaussian free field connectivity. Finally, a new method for measuring spectrogram accuracy is introduced, grounded in rigorous theoretical findings. These results are then used to develop a test for time-series data, enabling the detection of signals below the noise floor. The performance of this test is compared to existing signal detection methods, yielding competitive results. Notably, these results are superior when the period of the signal aligns with the width of the spectrogram window. A range of experimental studies were conducted, showcasing the efficacy of this new test in comparison to established methods. These studies included analyzing data from Earthquake ground acceleration, navigating through spectrograms with multiple frequencies, detecting periodic signals using spectrograms, and finally, obtaining precise period estimates using spectrogram levels. This module generates high-resolution maps of chaotic zones, which are characteristic of areas where the standard model of dust motion falls short, unable to accurately predict the random fluctuations experienced by particles in these regions. Each map is created by solving a stochastic differential equation, drawing from techniques used in stochastic process simulation methods, and is tailored for use in computational thermodynamic and hydrodynamic simulations. An alternative method is also provided, where the chaotic zone is modeled as an additive white Gaussian noise field, applicable in cases where the random fluctuation amplitude doesn't significantly impact the system's overall thermodynamic or hydrodynamic state. Both methods are showcased through model scenarios, including a demonstration of their use in simulating the acoustic phenomena observed in dusty winds. The module is open-source, providing researchers with a freely accessible tool to model additional physical processes. The open-source code is available at: https://git.iap.tu-dresden.de/voelkel/stochasticmodule/-/tree/master/stochastic_module_hdf5.py, with a detailed description provided in the associated README file. The module's performance is demonstrated in Section 3, where it is used to model a dusty wind as a case study, and finally, in Section 4, potential future applications are presented. In the end, in Section 5, the open-source code is confirmed to be effective, thoroughly validating its accuracy in highly turbulent environments. In the very end, in Section 6, the conclusions are drawn. In the very very end, in Section 7, the future prospects are presented.

Optical parametric oscillators represent a distinct category of nonlinear systems capable of generating idler and signal photons on demand, influencing the state of cavities through feedback control, and incorporating broad range of materials for various applications in quantum technology. For such systems, implementing feedback control is crucial but faces significant challenges due to fluctuations associated with the spontaneous scattering of photons. This research demonstrates the feasibility of feedback control in optical parametric oscillators trapped in cavities, overcoming these challenges by leveraging statistical properties of nonclassical light. By implementing a feedback algorithm based on homodyne measurement and incorporating memoryless scattering, the research enables adjustment of the optical parametric oscillator's loss threshold. This achievement marks a breakthrough in the application of feedback control to a wide range of nonlinear systems for quantum science and technology purposes. Additionally, the study's findings will contribute to the understanding of the dynamics of optical parametric oscillators.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. We discovered that DNase-I hypersensitive sites in specific cell types significantly influence many traits, indicating that ChIP data is particularly effective in pinpointing genes with functional importance. We also found that protein-coupled receptors, previously linked to certain disorders, are associated with multiple traits and are located near DNase-I hypersensitive sites that influence liver function, including factors related to obesity and metabolic diseases. Furthermore, exons of mRNAs, previously associated with certain disorders, are largely unconnected with most SNPs associated with other traits, suggesting limited regulatory relationships. This study provides new insights into the roles of different genomic elements in shaping human traits and disease-associated SNPs. We have made our method available to the public through a tool called annoci that includes a flexible software platform for computing associations between SNPs and any type of genomic element and can be used to investigate additional human traits and genomic elements by downloading the tool from the website. https://github.com/zhengjiny/annoci. For example, computing associations between 450 distinct genomic elements and eighteen human traits takes around two hours on a standard desktop computer. We have documented the steps to compute associations in the user manual available at https://github.com/zhengjiny/annoci/raw/master/docs/annoci_user_manual.pdf. This tool can also be used to investigate new data by incorporating new data sets for the same traits and studying novel biological pathways for human traits and disease-associated SNPs. In the future, we plan to extend our study to other species such as mouse and fly by using available ChIP data and exploring the functional roles of different genomic elements in shaping various organism characteristics. Ultimately, we aim to develop a method to predict the biological significance of any SNP based on available biological data. As this approach becomes increasingly applicable across various species and biological systems, it has the potential to significantly improve our ability to interpret disease-associated SNPs and design targeted therapeutic strategies. Similarly, this approach can significantly enhance our ability to predict the functional roles of novel variants

A non-trivial 2-design's automorphism group can either be an instance of the previously documented examples described in this research or a specific subgroup within a larger group of automorphisms that corresponds to a geometric linear transformation involving a prime number. Our analysis also establishes a relationship between a non-trivial 2-design's flag-transitive automorphism group and a geometric linear transformation involving a prime number, along with the previously documented examples. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their trajectory. Initially, we considered all possible velocity components, denoted by v_x and v_y, in the study of distant binary star systems with a short period. However, due to data limitations, only the line velocity, v_r, is typically analyzed in scientific research. Consequently, we examine the effectiveness of using the line velocity, v_r, in testing the law of gravity rather than using the full velocity distribution pattern, and found that using v_r is a suitable method for verifying gravitational consistency at the galactic edge. To compare the efficiency of using v_r and the full velocity distribution, the correlation coefficients of the velocity approaches, and v_r and the line-of-sight velocity, v_z, are calculated. Furthermore, the effectiveness of using v_r in testing the law of gravity is confirmed by using the velocity distribution pattern and v_z, in conjunction with data from 203 distant binary star systems. Moreover, the line-of-sight velocity, v_z, can be utilized in conjunction with data from 84 distant binary star systems to determine the velocity difference, v_r. Consequently, we discovered that using the line velocity, v_r, in conjunction with data from 203 distant binary star systems, supports the universality of Newton's gravitational law at the galactic edge. A sophisticated time series analysis tool called cross-correlation analysis is used in this study to explore the interconnected behaviors of time series, with a focus on financial markets. A novel prediction method for determining the future synchronization state of two related time series has been developed. Cross-recurrence plots are applied as a non-linear approach to measure the coupling between the time domain of two series, thus establishing their synchronization status. A deep learning strategy is employed to address the task of predicting synchronization states, utilizing dynamic sampling of cross-recurrence plots as key features. Experimental results from multiple stocks, including significant S&P 100 constituents, have been gathered to test the effectiveness of this method. Findings indicate that synchronizing predictions for time series pairs can be challenging, yet achieveable with substantial accuracy for certain stock pairs. Model ensembles and detailed analysis of results are presented to reinforce the study's validity. Information on model availability can be found in the paper's supplementary materials.

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior data, but face significant performance declines when confronted with new ads. To overcome this limitation, this study combines conventional methods with graph-based techniques, proposing an innovative framework called AdGraph. By incorporating graph embedding, AdGraph incorporates visual and text information from ads, and integrates this enhanced understanding into existing CTR models through feature merging. To minimize the cost of building graph models, AdGraph achieves this through dimension reduction, incorporating key image and text elements. Experimental results demonstrate that AdGraph surpasses traditional methods by 5-10% in terms of overall evaluation metrics, while also allowing for the rapid incorporation of new ads to enhance model performance. Notably, AdGraph's CTR predictions show improved consistency across different scales of ad exposure. To summarize, AdGraph's key advantages include its ability to efficiently handle new ads, improve CTR model accuracy, and enhance feature merging. It is worthy of note that AdGraph can be applied in online advertising industry to enhance the CTR prediction model. Traditionally, business process management concentrated on organized, task-based processes, but the rise in importance of intellectual work brings semi-organized processes into prominence. Current approaches for modeling business processes relying on in-depth knowledge often utilize information elements but fail to consider adequately the varying levels of such elements. As a result, these approaches can neither ensure the constraints related to information elements' levels are met, nor apply such constraints when dealing with simultaneous tasks and multiple process instances. This paper presents a new approach for modeling business processes relying on in-depth knowledge with dynamic information elements' levels. It defines a flexible process model that includes separate process flow and navigation logs. The proposed method includes navigation log formulas, allowing simultaneous tasks and multiple process instances to adhere strictly to the defined process flow. Nonetheless, the navigation log formulas may still lead to multiple feasible process flows, which can be calculated on the basis of dynamic constraint satisfaction. The method's applicability is validated through a practical example. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the applicability of the proposed method to real-life scenarios, such as a scholarship application process, utilizing a tool-supported case study. Finally, the paper reflects on the implemented prototype and outlines suggestions for future improvements. resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a need arises to adapt existing methods for wildfire AOD prediction
on a per-fire basis, considering varying dataset availability and accuracy.
This research proposes a new approach to develop a real-time wildfire AOD
prediction model using multiple data streams from various sources, even when
some streams may be unavailable due to satellite malfunctioning or coverage
limits. This method employs a novel combination of Bayesian statistical inference
and machine learning concepts, allowing the model to accommodate uncertainly
and make predictions as long as one valid input remains available.
This approach was tested using historical wildfire AOD data and future wildfire
maps for the state of California, with evaluations indicating that it can
effectively utilize diverse information sources and make precise predictions in
real-time, especially when compared to methods using individual data streams in
isolation. This methodology possesses universal applicability to problem areas
involving missing data and uncertainty in remote sensing-based environmental
monitoring, with potential applications extending to air quality, meteorological
systems, and more. This method has been successfully applied to predict AOD
resulting from the 2018 Camp Fire in California, with predictions showing
remarkable agreement with actual values, both during and after the fire. With

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. We illustrate the framework's efficacy in maintaining privacy for various scenarios, such as trajectories in a city or racetrack, maintaining a satisfactory balance between privacy and service accessibility. Our framework has potential applications in multiple fields, such as location-based services, statistics, and machine learning. Notably, our method differs from existing techniques in an important way: while existing techniques aim to maintain uniform distance between locations, our framework is designed to account for the actual relationships between those locations. Our proposed framework is versatile and can be utilized with various location models, such as GP and Markov models, providing a flexible solution to this complex problem. Our method has potential applications in multiple fields, such as location-based services, statistics, and machine learning. Our experiments using real data from Skating, Taxicab, and Peugeot demonstrate that our framework provides an advantage over protection methods that assume unrelated locations or use more conservative bounding techniques. Our results show that our framework enables us to maintain privacy with an entropy level up to $20\%$ higher than these other methods while delivering comparable distortion. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site variations affect our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies may actually enhance our statistical power to detect group differences while minimizing false positives. By simulating various conditions of within-group variability, we found that multisite studies have the beneficial effect of increasing our statistical power to detect group differences while constraining type I error rates. In contrast, single-site studies may yield false positives at increased rates due to the influence of within-site systematic errors. Our findings imply that multisite research can offer more accurate group difference identification and reduce false positive rates, representing a potential breakthrough in rsfMRI research. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained significant attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the issues posed by language switch, where words from different 
lingual origins often exhibit similar semantic properties. Building upon the 
success of fastText's pre-trained embeddings, this research extends this model 
by introducing a new pre-training approach, FastWord, aimed at generating 
meaningful word embeddings for code-mixed languages like Hinglish. The proposed 
methodical strategy addresses issues like out-of-vocabulary words and polysemous 
words by leveraging subword information and distinct linguistic origins, 
respectively. Experimental evaluations of the proposed model have yielded 
encouraging results, demonstrating its effectiveness in downstream NLP tasks 
such as sentiment analysis and question answering. Furthermore, this study 
investigates how the model's performance is affected by varying degrees of 
language mixing in the data. Experimental findings have also been substantiated 
by detailed qualitative analyses. Last but not least, the model has been used 
to identify word groups that demonstrate a strong connection between words 
regardless of their linguistic origins, thus highlighting the importance of 
considering language switching in NLP. Overall, the proposed model has shown 
remarkable potential in understanding code-mixed languages and their unique 
characteristics. As a testament to its effectiveness, the model has been 
open-sourced for public use. Additionally, the model has been successfully 
applied to understand similar language blends like Spanglish, another notable 
example of code-mixed languages. While the model has shown impressive 
performance, there is scope to further improve it by incorporating more 
advanced neural architectures such as ELMo and BERT in the future. Based on 
these findings, a new research direction has been identified, aiming to study 
how the characteristics of spoken languages affect their written forms and the 
quality of language models. As a contributing outcome, this research has 
presented an innovative way of visualizing the distribution of language 
mixing in large datasets, thus providing valuable insights to NLP researchers. 
Finally, the thesis has been successfully defended, marking a significant 
achievement, and the associated code and data have been made publicly 
available for reference purposes.

Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined these ideas somewhat abstractly. However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical analysis. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the weighted outcomes of a physical change in the genes of a homologous pair. We show that this apparent conflict can be resolved if specific relationships are maintained between gene frequencies and residual non-additive components, and also discuss the idea that maintaining causality as part of Fisher's original framework has certain advantages in the field. Fisher's key distinction between statistical correlation and causality holds crucial importance in the field of evolutionary biology and also for genetic studies of phenotypes. We apply this distinction to clarify the concepts of epistasis and quadratic epistasis, and demonstrate that the latter may simply be a manifestation of correlation, not causality. Furthermore, the idea that small-scale causal relationships between genes can be condensed into a linear relationship between gene frequencies and effects may not be applicable to larger scales such as entire gene groups or pools of genes. We also explore epigenetic silencing as an example of a causal relationship that can evolve through selection, but ultimately conclude that the distinction between correlation and causality remains complex and challenging to apply consistently to various forms of biological influence. Despite these difficulties, we suggest that maintaining causality as part of Fisher's original framework has certain advantages in the field. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and 3D geometric features simultaneously. A step-by-step camera relocalization pipeline is also suggested, utilizing a precomputed global database and generating pose estimates through minimization. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach under dual light sources. A related dataset, the Multi-view 3D Surfel Benchmark (M3S), is developed to evaluate benchmark performance. Federated learning is a decentralized AI technique that enables clients to collaborate on learning a common model without sharing their data. Each client uses the model sent by the server to process its local data and produces updated model parameters, but clients have limited labels, making it difficult to efficiently train their local models. With partially labeled data, clients must focus on filling in the missing labels for useful input information. This challenge is exacerbated by the potential for false class balances and unrepresentative data distribution. To address this issue, clients and the server must coordinate efficiently. This paper presents a new approach called L+N, where the server sends notifications to clients specifying which samples need more labels and guides them in filling in the missing labels. L+N also ensures that clients' local models are updated efficiently by combining their contributions. While clients focus on providing useful data, the server updates the model parameterally to stabilize convergence, using an adaptive weighted average of the updated models. Experiments show that L+N leads to superior performance and faster convergence compared to conventional federated learning methods. Additionally, L+N detects and mitigates data congestion caused by unrepresentative data on the clients. Based on these findings, L+N appears to be a viable solution for enhancing federated learning systems. This paper's novel ideas include using notification mechanisms from the server to guide client behavior and fill in missing labels efficiently, in addition to updating local models and detecting data congestion. Future research may apply L+N to various applications and modify its mechanisms to suit different use cases. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and mean accretion flow that dictate the post-merger behavior.  The contrast in the post-merger disk's magnetic and hydrodynamic states across simulations of different models, however, necessitates longer-term simulations to understand the disk's long-term behavior and its connection to the mass ejection and magnetic field dynamics.  The comparison of the initial neutron star models' influence on the post-merger disk state, also considered in this study, shows that an off-center initial model leads to a post-merger disk with greater radial extent and mass compared to an on-center model, suggesting that an off-center initial model could produce long-term magnetic and hydrodynamic similarities with an accretion disk surrounding a black hole and a companion star in a binary system.  The simulation findings, however, still disagree with observational microsecond-scale variations in the ultralight curve of the binary system GW170817, requiring more realistic models of the post-merger disk to explain these time variations.  The disagreement between simulation findings and ultralight curve data implies the necessity to study the post-merger disk using super-resolution methods in longer-term simulations or higher-resolution simulations up to at least $\sim 10^{-4}$ s duration to understand the origin of the observed time variations.  The consideration of a greater computational domain than the initial neutron star and its eccentric influence, also considered in this study, shows that an initial eccentricity of $\eta \approx 0.03$ leads to a mass ejection during the disruption of the neutron star that produces a universally similar accretion disk mass and profile compared to other simulations, indicating that high-energy radiation produced during the disruption could dominate the disruption process and mask the impact of initial eccentricity.  The consideration of a greater computational domain than the initial neutron star and its initial rotation, also considered in this study, shows that an initial rotation of $\beta \approx 0.70$ leads to a mass ejection during the disruption of the neutron star that produces a greater disk mass

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. Moreover, we apply the findings to a specific context, specifically the study of a random walk on a cube with a rapidly changing even perspective, to determine that a conditioned random walk on a cube converges uniformly to a specific Markov process and thereby attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium. Finally, we establish that the speed of convergence in this instance is a function of the inverse of the square root of the time. Jointly published with the main paper, this note addresses several additional questions regarding quasi-stationary distributions and their applications in the study of random walks on a cube (illustrating the complexity of general random walks on a dynamical even perspective, for example). An appendix is included to address a specific question regarding the convergence of the average perspective. Additionally, an independent study is presented in a separate paper titled Random walks on a cube with perspectives subject to dynamic changes (arXiv 2101.00073). Specifically, it was found that the set of all even perspectives on the cube is group-generated and that there exist perspectives that allow a random walk on the cube to spend a proportionate amount of time in any given sub-set of the cube under certain conditions. A fundamental approach is presented in the study, along with applications to the manifolds of Rubik's Cube and Chirality of Drosophila. Moreover, a random walk on a cube with perspectives that are mutually reciprocal and dynamically changing is shown to be asymptotically independent of a rapid Markov process. Finally, the asymptotic independence is also demonstrated in a group of perspectives that are dynamically changing and mutually reciprocal on the torus and the surface of a ball. In addition, the relationship between the speed of a random walk on a cube that is dynamically changing and the exponential rate at which it approaches its quasi-stationary equilibrium was found to be directly proportional to the square root of the time. A comparable result was also found for a random walk on a dynamically changing torus where the speed of the random walk is related to the time by a power of one-half. This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. Our findings demonstrate that the excitation of graphene's surface plasmons can generate a repulsive force that overcomes attraction, leading to particle rotation. Additionally, we found that the speed of rotation is controlled by the graphene's chemical potential and that thermal energy can increase the probability of rotation above room temperature. Ultimately, our model provides a framework for graphen-assisted optical manipulation and offers potential applications in NMR magnetometry. [From the article's abstract]

Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; however, increasing this timeframe may lead to unintended consequences, such as increased hospital lengths of stay and higher costs. To investigate these effects, we applied an econometric analysis to data from a hospital treating abdominal pain patients. The study found that prolonging the treatment time to 230 minutes is optimal for maximizing admissions, and this benefit can be fully captured within the first 75 minutes of extension. The study's results align with those of prior research, indicating that the value of improving discharge times is substantial, at $1200 per patient, and that these effects are largely driven by variations in length of stay. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on situations where the overall cost function is unique and shared equally among agents. The question we address is whether multiple agent actions can be synchronized to minimize total cost, under the condition that all agents make informed decisions. The answer depends on the specific system configuration, but a collective achievement is possible if all agents act in unison, and a individual success is possible if all other agents cooperate. The absence of collective or individual success indicates a system fault. The action choices of multiple agents can be synchronized to minimize total cost, a state that translates to a Nash equilibrium characterized by two distinct conditions. First, the overall cost incurred by each agent must be equal, indicating a mutual agreement to divide costs equally among themselves. Second, any deviation by an agent must result in a higher total cost for that agent, thereby reinforcing the current action distribution. The time taken by each agent to reach this distribution can be unpredictable, but once achieved, it remains stable. The application of linear dynamic systems that produce a unique outcome aligns with our definition of cooperative systems, under the condition that all agents make fully informed decisions. Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that cancel out CME signal produced results consistent with zero for certain collision energies and peripherality classes, while a significant CME signal remained for the most peripheral collisions. Ultimately, the largest CME signal was found for collisions with the lowest collision energy and the greatest peripherality. Additionally, the study found that the leading collisions in the charge correlator calculated based on odd parity particles followed a distinct trend depending on collision energy. Specifically, the effect was more pronounced in lower-energy collisions. Furthermore, the study discovered that the leading collisions in the charge correlator calculated based on even parity particles displayed the least variation in both collision energy and peripherality. Specifically, the effect became more pronounced in higher-energy collisions. Finally, the integrals of both correlators exhibited distinct variations in both collision energy and peripherality. Specifically, the effect became more pronounced in higher-energy collisions for the correlator calculated based on even parity particles, while it did so for the correlator calculated based on odd parity particles at lower energies. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of Traversal Problem from Graph Theory, with a focus on completing tasks in an optimal order. While successful, this approach faces a major challenge in real-time contexts: optimizing task execution times. This paper explores an alternative strategy for reducing task processing times, by scheduling tasks in a different order based on their completion times. This approach shares similarities with the Permutation Flowshop Scheduling Problem and can be associated with the Traversal Problem. However, the focus here lies in reducing task processing times rather than optimizing the schedule directly. This variant's complexity was confirmed to be NP-hard, using a reduction from the Quadratic Boolean Partitioning Problem. A algorithm incorporating approximate methods, such as Random Search and Gradient Descent, is proposed, along with performance guarantees and a parameterization for adjusting solution quality. Experimental results validate the performance of this algorithm in both simulated and real-world settings, where it is compared to standard graph traversal algorithms. Furthermore, the paper presents a method for adjusting the algorithm to handle a sequence of tasks that are subject to change. When tasks are modified or deleted, the algorithm can adapt through a process involving reinforcement learning, as evidenced by experimental results. Finally, the paper investigates the potential for applying this algorithm to a mobile manipulator, by evaluating its efficiency in a simulated environment inspired by the Co-Taobao benchmark. While the algorithm offers competitive performance, it is susceptible to significant slowdowns when handling a large number of tasks. This discrepancy suggests that the algorithm may be more suited to applications where tasks are executed at a steady pace. Conversely, graph traversal algorithms prove more versatile, while the between-task time adjustment strategy shows promise for its potential to improve performance in similar applications. Furthermore, the paper presents a new approach for reducing the impact of irregularities in task execution times, by adjusting the order in which tasks are completed. By combining this strategy with the previously mentioned algorithms, the paper discovers a new algorithm with reduced dependence on task processing times. Finally, the paper explores the potential for applying this new variant, as well as the original, to a mobile manipulator in a steady-state environment. While the original variant proves uncompetitive, the new variant presents a more promising outlook, outperforming the standard graph traversal algorithm in some instances. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method has been employed to mitigate this issue, however, it is often based on an equal allocation of labels, which leads to low-quality pseudo-labels dominating the node classification process, resulting in poor performance. In contrast, this research proposes an Informational Pseudo-Labeling Framework (IPLF) to tackle the problem of label scarcity in GNNs. IPFL first calculates the predictive confidence for each node, then assigns pseudo-labels based on confidence levels, with high-confidence nodes labeled first to maximize impact. Additionally, IPFL mitigates the effects of negative pseudo-labels by implementing a node grouping approach. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IPFL in outperforming existing methods with limited labels. Notably, IPFL achieves comparable performance to models with a full set of labels when the budget is expanded to 128. The source code is available at https://github.com/juynp/InfoPL. We present a generic, classical modeling of electric circuits that describes conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, where a mechanical oscillator functions as a mobile capacitor within a parallel RLC circuit. By deriving an equivalent circuit model, we illustrate how the fundamental optomechanical principles can be realized through electrostatic forces between the mechanical oscillator and the microresonator, as well as damping effects resulting from electrical connections. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this classical model aligns with the well-established quantum optomechanics when the mechanical oscillator's displacement variables and position states are represented as Wigner functions. By performing phase-space evolution of the Wigner function, we derive the equations of motion for the specific single-tone microwave optomechanics system. Ultimately, our classical model facilitates a straightforward transition from quantum to classical treatment, thereby enhancing simulation efficiency and flexibility. Additionally, we show that optomechanical phenomena can be reliably reproduced from purely classical means, including hysteresis and bistability. oscillating or weaving pattern. We demonstrate that a simple model can simulate these

Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited coherence times. We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may have distorted or delayed reflections. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, taking into account the timing and amplitude of signal components, including direct and indirect paths. This approach utilizes an adaptable noise model to account for varying signal conditions. We have implemented a Python-based solution that mimics the ADALM-PLT board's protocol for exchanging data between a board and a computer, which serves as a key application of our method. We have also conducted simulations to evaluate our algorithm under different scenarios, including varying signal strengths and distortion rates, which have shown significantly improved localization accuracy. Notably, our method exhibits enhanced performance even in situations where a significant percentage of signals is delayed or distorted. Furthermore, our algorithm demonstrates the ability to adapt to changing signal conditions, including varying distances between the mobile object and anchors. The average time taken by the algorithm to converge is approximately 0.2 milliseconds. Detailed evaluation results, including graphs and tables, are available for download on our project website. The implemented solution has a total memory usage of approximately 0.05 megabytes. We believe our method provides an efficient and accurate solution for mobile object localization that can adapt to various signal conditions. This approach has broad potential applications in areas such as robotics, tracking systems, and location-based services. The complete source code presented here can be utilized as a benchmark or modified for different purposes. We intend to extend our work in future by incorporating real-world data collected from mobile devices. The source code is available on our website for public use. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Additionally, this system facilitates the review and modification of proofs on paper. We further demonstrate the potential of this visual representation by outlining a method for utilizing it in the instruction and review of proof-based subjects. We share the result of this research as a Coq library, named VisualProof, which contains a number of tutorials and documentation to aid in its use. We also present four, five-page, visual proofs of significant mathematical theorems, dealing with subjects such as algebra, arithmetic, number theory, and real analysis. These visual proofs, along with the associated full Coq proof scripts, are available at the VisualProof library. Lastly, we highlight four prospective uses for this visual representation, as well as the potential benefits and research questions associated with each use. However, in some scenarios, different teams within an organization use varying process models to represent their individual business processes. Consequently, it is necessary to develop a method that can simultaneously monitor and evaluate multiple process models. Our proposed approach, BPs, enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple business process models, aligned with the same clinical business process, under monitored business processes. To illustrate the practical applications of our method, we will utilize an example from the medical field. According to recent research, approximately 30-50% of clinical guidelines contain ambiguous or unclear statements known as 'rule ambiguities.' These ambiguities make it challenging for doctors to apply clinical guidelines in patient treatment and increase the risk of errors. To address these issues, we will define and demonstrate a new type of rule, referred to as the F-Rule, along with an algorithm designed to identify and solve 'guideline ambiguities' during business process instance execution. Our method, BPs, can now handle different types of F-Rules, including data-dependent and data-independent types. Our method, BPs, can now handle up to P instances of F-Rules. Our experimental results confirm these findings, using real-world data from the medical field. Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables the description of quantum circuits by embedding in Haskell, resulting in a highly functional and practical language. Yet, its embedded nature in Haskell hinders the development of a formal semantics and restricts the type system. The absence of linear types in Haskell makes it simple to write quantum state-cloning violating code. The Proto-Quipper family addresses this issue through research languages designed to ensure the type-safety of quantum circuit fragments. Specifically, this paper examines Proto-Quipper-M, which employs a categorical quantum circuit model and incorporates linear types for compile-time cloning property verification. The study then develops a small-step operational semantics by transforming its corresponding big-step model and proves their equivalence. Following these proofs, it proves subject reduction and progress results for a derived small-step operational semantics. The resulting abstract machine-style small-step semantics is eventually demonstrated to be equivalent to the original model. The research provides a fundamental framework for evaluating type-preserving compile-time optimisations in quantum circuit fragments. The development is accompanied by formal proofs, which can be found on the CodeMap platform. The paper further discusses type-preserving compile-time optimisations and the potential for future work in the quantum programming domain. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the remaining sequences are processed using a de Bruijn graph assembler to produce the fully assembled genome. By eliminating unnecessary nodes in the graph, the proposed approach achieves significant cost reduction and improves performance, ultimately resulting in faster genome assembly times. Experimental results on multiple genomes reveal that this new method, SGA-Sparse, surpasses current leading assembler tools in terms of speed and scalability, while maintaining comparable accuracy. SGA-Sparse is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/alejinhos/SGA-Sparse.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel HDR Lasso solution that takes full advantage of the problem's sparse nature. Our proposed Adaptive Sieving High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (ASHDR Lasso) algorithm is an efficient method for solving the HDR Lasso problem, which has been extensively tested through simulated studies. When compared to alternative approaches, the ASHDR Lasso model demonstrated superior performance in terms of estimation accuracy, computational speed, and the ability to detect relevant features. To validate the effectiveness of the ASHDR Lasso in real-world applications, we applied the method to analyze the gene expression data from three distinct cancer studies, verifying the method's ability to identify relevant genes and replicate results accurately. When compared to other approaches, the ASHDR Lasso model successfully detected known risk genes and replicated study-specific findings, underscoring the method's potential for biocausal research and analysis. When applied to real-world gene expression data, the ASHDR Lasso model successfully detected known risk genes and replicated study-specific findings, demonstrating the method's potential for biocausal research and analysis. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown using sequencing data from multiple time points. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. We applied this model to ER-alpha activated cells from a breast cancer line, analyzing transcription using ChIP-Seq data and mature RNA quantities from mRNA-Seq data. The results show that a considerable number of genes exhibit a prolonged period between transcription completion and mature RNA production. Furthermore, genes exhibiting longer delays are typically shorter and are associated with retained introns in pre-mRNA data, suggesting significant production delays attributed to splicing events. The developed approach is highly versatile, suitable for use with various Nucleotide-Count data from distinct sources, such as experiments, models, or simulations. Firstly, it facilitates the rapid evaluation of functions determined by a fixed set of input variables. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening. Typically, these materials respond to increased stress by transitioning from a fluid-like to a more solid-like state, despite generally presenting a fluidic appearance. Research suggests that during this transition, the nature of particle-particle interactions that previously contributed to fluidity shifts towards causing rigidity. We explored a novel type of suspension, comprising equal parts polystyrene spheres and a liquid-like substance, to which a special agent was added to ensure that all particles at the microlevel maintain equal interactions. Under specific conditions, this suspension behaves as a fluid, but when subjected to high stresses in a specific alignment, it undergoes a sudden thickening, causing the fluidity to cease temporarily. Notably, the particles in the solid-like state cause waves to form on their surface, as if solidified. We, then, investigated the mechanism of the thickening transition in the static regime by adjusting stress levels. X-ray scattering data revealed that during the thickening process, particles cause waves on the liquid's surface, forming a semi-solid state characterized by a specific interparticle distance, thus indicating the onset of temporary, stress-level-dependent constraints on particle movement. Additionally, the extent of particle-causing waves increases with the stress levels. We discovered that the transition from a fluid to a semi-solid state in our experiments is independent of the concentration of the particles. Furthermore, the application of our findings to other types of suspensions, including those composed of living cells, reveals a common pattern in the thickening process, as demonstrated through the analysis of the shear-induced thickening of red blood cells. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. The proposed LoraR (L.O.R.A.R.) framework addresses these difficulties by providing a standardized approach to LoraR analysis. The LoraR framework consists of three components: representation, transformation, and interpretation. The website lorr.fr serves as a resource, offering guidance, code repositories (primarily in R), and educational materials. The primary goal of the LoraR framework is to standardize the conceptual foundation for future research into LoraR analysis, as well as the development of associated methods, applications, and software. The proposed standard recognizes the diversity of practical problems while also facilitating the exchange of ideas, methods, and software across disciplines. Staying true to the spirit of Bouza-Casarrubias et al. (2020), the proposed standard represents a compromise between breadth and depth, as well as flexibility and formality. The proposed standard is intended to be dynamic, designed to be reviewed, updated, and revised regularly in response to feedback from the community. The proposed standard has already received input from approximately 150 individuals and has undergone approximately 30 revisions to date. The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory. 

In this research, we provide further empirical evidence to support this conclusion by analyzing the exoplanet mass distribution at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with varying orbital periods, which shows a continuous rather than biphasic characteristic. By using POPs (Pseudo-Major Axis Planets) as a suitable statistical tool (Mordasini et al., 2009), we isolate and quantify the effects of H$_2$ dominated accretion and shearing forces that may influence the mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets. 

We discovered that high-mass exoplanets with short orbital periods are characterized by high densities, which is consistent with H$_2$ dominated accretion leading to smaller final cores. However, rather than biphasic barycentric masses, which is consistent with the core accretion scenario, we find a continuous relation between exoplanet mass and distance from the parent star. This is likely due to a bipolar mass distribution among stars (e.g. Harper et al., 2017) rather than bipolar planet formation processes. 

Additionally, we explore the impact of shearing forces that may strip away angular momentum from exoplanets, which indicates that satellites with low inclinations and high eccentricities are stripped of their angular momentum through tidal interactions, which may lead to circular orbits. Which in turn, could result in super-Earths and sub-neptunian planets with close proximate orbits. 

Bearing these constraints, which may influence the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets, we find that core accretion is the predominant formation process, which is consistent with the known properties of exoplanets rather than biphasic character as suggested previously.

We investigate how these models allocate their "attention" when faced with abundant input information during training. We also develop a method called Attention Shaping, which utilizes auxiliary training signals to influence attention patterns and utilize supplementary inputs more effectively. While Attention Shaping leads to improved task performance in certain scenarios, its benefits disappear when the system has unrestricted access to all inputs. A theoretical model, called $f^2{\cal R}^2$, is studied as a quantum gravity candidate in a scenario where Standard Model fermions acquire mass through the breaking of a $U(1)_B$ symmetry. In this model, at low fermion densities, a condensed dark matter candidate can form in a supersymmetric vacuum, exhibiting either Bose-Einstein condensation or Wigner molecular phase, depending on the number of fermions. In the presence of an external magnetic field, a complex phase consisting of a supersymmetric critical phase and a Wigner molecular phase can occur, given that a critical density condition is met. Additionally, for sufficiently high fermion density, a supersymmetric vacuum can display magnetic susceptibility, ultimately transitioning to a supersymmetric dual photon phase. Furthermore, for sufficiently strong magnetic field and high fermion density, a supersymmetric vacuum can display magnetic compressibility, ultimately exhibiting a supersymmetric Higgs phase. In all phases, quantum gravity fluctuations are accounted for, and it is found that they affect the susceptibility, compressibility, and critical temperatures of the model. Specifically, the quantum gravity effect on the critical temperatures shows that it can differsignificantly from the known quantum gravity induced critical temperatures of the Standard Model. Moreover, the quantum gravity effect on the dark matter candidate can exhibit a high density limit, in contrast to the standard high density limit. Finally, potential detection methods for the model phases are discussed. Potential experiments that can detect the model phases include: (i) a neutrino-less double beta decay experiment in the 0νβδ mode can detect the supersymmetric critical phase. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and brain area connections, which brain algorithms (locality) can help overcome. We developed locality-masked RNNs (LM-RNNs) by incorporating these constraints into RNNs, resulting in significant training efficiency improvements and lower memory requirements. We observed high similarity rates between optimal LM-RNNs and fully-connected RNNs, especially in problem types that fully-connected RNNs perform well in, such as navigation and counterexamples. Additionally, LM-RNNs showed superior data efficiency compared to fully-connected RNNs. We proposed a bio-realistic training protocol and demonstrated the success of LM-RNNs in learning and transferring skills across related tasks. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for developing more advanced RNN models inspired by brain connectivity and learning mechanisms. We also provide an open-source implementation of locality-masked RNNs (https://github.com/ethereality/CMU_BioRL_GoLang) that can be easily integrated into existing deep learning frameworks. Our research includes supplementary materials and a video presentation available at https://cmu-biorl.github.io/. We conducted an online survey to share our findings with the neurosciences and machine learning communities (https://osf.io/3j39g/). Ultimately, our goal is to foster a collaborative relationship between these two communities to develop new, more efficient, and more practical RNN models inspired by the brain's functional architecture. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to coordinate and intensity inversions. These enhanced feature properties are integrated into symmetric kernel-based point-wise registration, modeled using binary feature correspondence. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the development of diverse and tailored transport plans, this framework provides a thorough understanding of global pooling, thereby enabling the creation of more sophisticated and effective global pooling layers. Specifically, a new global averaging layer is proposed, which maintains calculational simplicity and can be easily integrated into a wide range of models, including ResNet, MobileNet, and DenseNet. Through rigorous testing, the performance of the proposed layer has been compared with other global averaging methods, and the results show that it achieves superior accuracy and efficiency while incurring minimal computational costs. Notably, the proposed layer surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art models such as EfficientNet and RegNetY, resulting in a 0.7% and 1.3% improvement in image classification tasks, respectively, with equivalent computational efficiency. The code for the proposed method has been made available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/global-pooling. Additionally, the related project information can be accessed at https://qianhewu.github.io/Global-Pooling/. Furthermore, the relevant data sets can be found at https://github.com/Qianhewu/global-pooling/tree/master/datasets. Lastly, the relevant paper can be accessed at https://www.qianhewu.github.io/papers/Global-Pooling.pdf.

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER or Type 2 nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxies. These results contradict the unified model, and suggest that there's a symbiotic relationship between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges. Furthermore, our analysis shows that spiral host galaxies with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei predominantly face towards the observer, whereas the distribution of Type 2 Seyfert nuclei orientations aligns with those of LINER and non-AGN galaxies, suggesting a diversity of orientation-dependent mechanisms. Additionally, our investigation indicates that galactic bar widths do not significantly vary according to AGN classification. Conversely, and in contrast to previous studies, we did not discover major differences in the sizes of galactic bulges hosting AGN compared to non-AGN nuclei. Our analysis also shows that galactic mass, as indicated by the stellar mass, is not a factor that explains the observed trends in AGN host galaxy morphology. Furthermore, our investigation indicates that galactic star formation rates, as classified by the SDSS, are insensitive to AGN classification. However, in contrast to other stages in the AGN lifecycle, the observed trends in elliptical galaxies hosting AGN resemble those of galaxies undergoing a transition from star-forming to quiescent activity. Our data suggest that the transition of AGN from spiral to elliptical hosts occurs around the LINER phase, and that the well-known trend of AGN 'quenching' may also imply a role for black hole activity in suppressing star formation in galaxies. In the long-term, our findings suggest that the active black hole, particularly in elliptical galaxies, may be the remnants of a dormant supermassive black hole created by the merger of two galactic nuclei. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanically written stories with limited creativity. In contrast, neural models used in natural language generation tasks are capable of more imaginative storytelling, but their applicability to time-series data has been limited due to the complexity and custom nature of such data. A new framework, called TheCube (TCube), utilizes neural networks to generate time-series inspired narratives without requiring any template adjustments. TCube's versatility allows it to work with various time-series datasets by incorporating external, semi-external, or internal context, outperforming other neural approaches in terms of coherence and interestingness in narrative generation. Furthermore, our system's relevance is validated through user evaluations that prefer the generated stories over those produced by traditional methods. With its innovative design, TCube holds great promise for applications involving time-series data and significant advances in state-of-the-art neural story generation technologies. This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which exhibit polynomial or unbounded behavior. Our investigations involve two scenarios: equations with polynomial growth and those with unbounded growth. For the first case, we introduce a new smoothing quantity and leverage it to demonstrate the solution's dependence on the initial data and establish an $L^2$ estimate. For the second scenario, we introduce a new time-dependent metric on the phase space and use it to obtain key estimates, which in turn allow us to probe the regularity of solutions. Interestingly, our findings indicate that, in both scenarios, the loss of regularity is inherent and related to the nature of the equation, rather than a consequence of the metric. Specifically, in the case of moderate blow-up, the loss is limited to $H^1$ regularity, whereas in the case of unbounded growth, the loss extends to $H^2$ regularity. Furthermore, we show that this loss is an inherent feature of the problem by supplanting an existing $L^2$ estimate for solutions with an unconditional $L^2$ estimate for derivatives, thus highlighting the metric's influence. Additionally, we leverage the proposed time-dependent metric to obtain essential insights, including the non-degeneracy of the phase space and the boundedness of energy estimates, which contribute to understanding the equation's behavior. Notably, our investigations indicate that, in both scenarios, the phase space remains non-degenerate and the equation's energy estimates remain bounded, thus precluding the possibility of developing a coercive boundary condition. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the well-posedness, dependence on initial data, loss of regularity, and phase space properties for a broad class of strictly hyperbolic equations with moderate blow-up coefficients. Furthermore, our findings offer insights into the function theory of linear equations, as well as connections to the research field of hyperbolic equations with unbounded coefficients. Additionally, our conclusions may be applied to various classes of partial differential equations, including the study of the $b$-hyperbolic equation and the generalized Klein-Gordon equation. On Stack Overflow, users frequently utilize links to share resources, including official documentation, tutorials, and other external information. These links can be considered a form of external expertise shared among users, enhancing the knowledge base within the Q&A platform. Despite their importance, understanding the role of links shared on Stack Overflow is limited to the information provided by users who post the links, which restricts their potential impact. By assuming that linked documents are consistently represented by the titles or descriptions provided, or in some cases by the shared code, we overlook the opportunities for collaborative knowledge development. In an effort to uncover the extent of this limitation, we carried out a study on Stack Overflow's link sharing activities. Our results indicate that only a small proportion of these links point to external resources, while a significant number refer to official documentation, tutorials, and other knowledge-sharing activities. Given the central role of links shared on Stack Overflow, we also examined the measures used to indicate their quality and functionality, which reveal a considerable deficiency. These links are often verified as functional, but even among the non-functional ones, users indicate that the associated documents or resources may still be useful. By comparing the information provided to those with expertise, we found that users estimate the link's quality based on the description of the linked resource, rather than the actual URL, thus highlighting the potential for improving current measures. We have created the initial edition of SIDDm, a web-based tool that allows for exploring Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) models by adjusting simulation parameters based on a specific set of observations. Compared to Cold Dark Matter (CDM) models, SIDM models have a distinct sensitivity to baryonic feedback processes. To compare these models effectively, we have developed SIDDm, which includes a variety of simulation options and observation-based constraints. Users can input parameters into SIDDm to generate contours representing the consistency of the models with empirical data, specifically galaxy rotation curve observations. Additionally, SIDDm enables users to run simulations for specific galaxies and view the resulting curves for further analysis. Currently, the tool is capable of handling galaxies with stellar masses ranging from $10^{6}$ to $10^{10}$ solar masses and is available at [siddm.org](siddm.org) for free use by researchers. Future updates to SIDDm will incorporate user feedback to enhance its functionality and add novel features. Furthermore, SIDDm's source code is openly available on GitHub for potential contributors to improve the tool. We welcome suggestions and encourage users to share their feedback to help make SIDDm an invaluable resource for researchers. We intend to maintain and expand SIDDm to cover a broader range of observations and simulation outcomes, ultimately making it a valuable and indispensable tool for scientists. Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
the knowledge base and its code will be made open-source for the scientific community. Evaluation outcomes demonstrate
that our system's recommended values-based communication outperform baseline approaches in engaging users and
stimulating valuable conversations. Conversely, our knowledge base shows strengths in its extensive coverage of climate topics.

illustrating the potential of technological innovations to address complex global challenges like climate change.

Incorporating our knowledge-based climate communication, designers can create more effective tools to combat climate change, 
enhancing the potential for individual actions and widespread adoption.
