on computational clusters managed by Stanford's Center for Research on Learning and
Education.  Our results can be found at:  http://musictheory.stanford.edu/  [1].

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately from the ones that merged with existing groups. The items integrating with existing groups lead to smaller, interconnected groups, whereas separate initiation results in the emergence of larger, separate groups, thereby producing a hierarchical structure. We establish asymptotic expressions for the probability that a given item starts a new group separately from those merging with existing groups, by means of analyzing a comb-like sequence. We demonstrate that the primary factor governing this probability is the local density of the item-set it is added to. The successive intervals possess distinct parameters driving this probability, which is found to be equivalent to the sequence's central term as the sequence evolves. Consequently, we derive an explicit expression for this central term, which reveals that it depends on the sequence's underlying distribution function. The derived expressions are applied to investigate specific instances, such as the uniform distribution, where the probability sequence converges to a specific expression involving the sequence's index and the harmonic series. The applied results also include an analysis of the discrepancy between the applied probabilities and the local density, which shows that this discrepancy can be approximated using an alternative probability sequence. The studied class of stochastic processes encompasses a broad category, including label avoidance processes, where a specific label is refrained from assignment in the sequence. By means of analyzing the local density, we establish the probability of label avoidance, as well as derive expressions for the probability of two distinct labels, $a$ and $b$, being refrained from in the sequence. Furthermore, we apply the derived expressions to investigate specific instances, such as the uniform distribution, where the probability of a specific label being refrained from can be precisely determined. The studied class of stochastic processes, as well as the derived expressions and applications, share notable parallels with the growth of distinct vocabulary in a linguistic hierarchy, where a newly discovered word is added to an existing word, either by a contraction, initiating separately from the contracting words, or through a merger of separate words. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. By harbingers, we show that the harmony condition derives naturally from a more fundamental notion, and through which, demonstrate the equivalence of the inversion and recovery principles in a more organic manner. Additionally, we address the prevailing interpretation of the inversion principle as failing in a notable instance, known as the Barantsev example. By reevaluating the example, we show that the harmony condition allows for a more balanced assessment. Finally, we sketch the potential implications of the harmony condition on the design of dedicated proof systems. Currently, an open question revolves around determining whether the harmony condition is sufficient to derive the contraction-free version of the harmony condition. If met, this would enable the development of proof systems tailored to avoid contraction. Conversely, if failed, it would necessitate an approach distinct from cut-elimination, perhaps via a dedicated dedicated proof engine. In either case, we believe the harmony condition offers valuable insights into the intricate relationship between computation and proof. In particular, we show that the harmony condition fails in the lambda calculus when interpreted as requiring the preservation of subproofs, albeit Combinatorial Ludics satisfies this interpretation. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method remains effective in scenarios where the underlying system dynamics are non-stationary. To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach called Region Learning, which utilizes deep reinforcement learning to identify the optimal action policies within the defined regions. Notably, we find that RL agents can reliably replicate comparisons from prior human sessions, thereby effectively closing knowledge gaps between their current and past performance. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. These simulations evaluate the impact of varying'm' values on estimator performance and compare them with traditional maximum likelihood estimates. The method is implemented in an R function, available through the R package Extreme. A real-life application using data from Cumbria is also presented to demonstrate its effectiveness. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving RL known as the robust offline multi-arm bandits. We aim to find a learning algorithm that can provide a guarantee on performance in the worst case, given that the adversary may manipulate a portion $\beta$ of data in the training set. Our proposed algorithm achieves a $O(\sqrt{\ln T} + \mbox{poly}(1/\beta))$ regret guarantee, which is consistent with the lower bound of $O(\sqrt{\ln T})$. Notably, we demonstrate that a significant improvement in robustness can be achieved by incorporating additional data, which is a key consideration in RL. We explore the more challenging setting of robust online RL, which involves the consideration of an adversary that can adaptively modifies data in each time step. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm. Furthermore, we extend these results to a multi-dimensional heat equation under constant boundary conditions, proving the existence and uniqueness of the minimum L^2-norm impulsive control and implementing an efficient algorithm to achieve these controls. Our study includes numerical examples that validate the performance of the developed algorithm in obtaining the minimum L^2-norm impulsive control. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address impulsive control in the exact version of the 1-D heat equation with dynamic boundaries and also presents new findings on the impulsive approximation control of the 1-D heat equation with dynamic boundaries, the exact version of the multi-dimensional heat equation, and the standard multi-dimensional heat equation. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. Furthermore, we proposed a proposal system for evaluating methods in future research, with the goal of promoting and discovering effective methods for detecting out-of-distribution examples. Additionally, our work highlighted potential pitfalls in reliance on anchor weights, corruptions, and semi-supervised settings that may compromise fairness and generalizability in evaluations. In contrast, we found that relying on ten percent hold-out data proved to be both unbiased and precise in assessing model performance. Based on these findings, we suggested that future research prioritize developing more comprehensive and few-shot diagnostic tools for measuring model generalizability and fairness. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet subsequent analyses throughout the 2000s produced mixed results. Recent advancements in the data analysis technique SPECS allow for more accurate spectrophal analysis, and we have re-examined the data from the study by Oppenheimer et al. (1999) to gain a revised understanding of the properties of GJ 229B. By employing a new data generation approach and a Bayesian reconstruction method to remove instrumental biases, we have revised the estimates of the mass and effective temperature of GJ 229B. Our research indicates that the mass of the dwarf, initially estimated as 55 ± 10 MJ, now stands at 46 ± 13 MJ. Correspondingly, its temperature has been revised from 723 ± 30 K to 684 ± 63 K. Despite these modifications, the middle-to-long wave faintness issues of GJ 229B remain unaddressed. Furthermore, our findings still indicate a strong requirement for the presence of a heavy element, specifically silicon, in the dwarf's atmosphere. To resolve the instrumental biases affecting the data, we suggest combining the speckle images of the system with empirical models of the human eye or alternative image reconstruction methods. Nonetheless, our primary conclusion regarding the peculiar spectral behavior of GJ 229B remains unchanged, implying that it may be composed of condensed silicon and carbon materials or that its atmospheric composition is unusually different from that of other T-dwarfs in the nearby solar neighborhood. To confirm this, we require precise spectral analysis of multiple objects, and the estimated instrumental limit of SPECS ($10^{-4}$ R$_{\odot}$) is insufficient; thus, we suggest that future observations of GJ 229B should be conducted with a $0.3"$ field-of-view using instruments with spectrally flat response in the $5.0$-$25.0$ $\mu m$ interval. Additionally, we propose that speaking clearly and using simple word choices in scientific communication can aid in the reduction of cognitive biases and contribute to the development of innovative ideas. Finally, mission designers should prioritize the incorporation of a blue optical filter in future microscopes to reduce glare and enable precise observation of planetary systems.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used reliable tools to model and analyze virus-laden aerosol transport. Bus ventilation was simulated through a combination of factors such as ventilation systems, occupancy rates, driving speed, wind resistance, and individual respiratory or expiratory actions. When a passenger on board coughs or sneezes, the aerosol plume is dispersed by local air currents created by wind resistance, while also being affected by the bus's ventilation. To assess the extent to which these aerosols are circulated, we conducted experiments using laser-induced fluorescence techniques to measure and evaluate the mean age and dispersal of aerosols under various conditions. Based on our findings, the risk of airborne transmission on a bus appears to be minimal when it is in motion and the ventilation system is functioning properly. However, the risk increases when the bus is stationary, due to air stagnation. Therefore, to minimize the risk of transmission on a bus, it is essential to maintain a fresh air supply, much like in hospitals, and to increase ventilation coefficients by opening windows and using heat exchangers. Additionally, passengers should refrain from gathering in groups and standing close to each other to minimize personal air exchange. For a period of time equivalent to five minutes of continuous exposure on an bus in motion, the required distance between passengers to minimize transmission risk would need to be at least 10 meters (33 feet) apart. All of these measures should be implemented to create a safe and healthy travel environment on the bus. Furthermore, our study's focus on both healthy and unwell individuals allows for the application of these findings to other enclosed environments as well. By simulating the environment of a doctor's consultation room, we found the risk of transmission to be significantly higher than in a bus, and thus in need of further investigation. To facilitate a safe and healthy interaction between patients and doctors, a healthy air exchange rate in a consultation room would require a significant and constant fresh air supply, much like in hospitals. As an added precaution, the risk of transmission could also be minimized by installing filters in ventilation systems in such areas as well. Nonetheless, the primary factor influencing the transport of virus-laden aerosols in enclosed environments appears to be the efficiency of air exchange rate. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested our methods using an event stream processor designed to monitor real-time financial data. Specifically, we used the Kibana dashboard to analyze the AWS IPO, while our event stream processor detected key events including the moment when stock prices surpassed their target. Furthermore, our approach successfully identified the correct timing of these events as well as the moment when stock price gaps occurred. To provide further insight into the functionality of our system, a video detailing its operation is available at https://youtu.be/ISOsVCfzBfM. From this video, we learned that the average time taken by our verification system to process each detected event was under 50 milliseconds. To summarize, our work made three significant contributions to the field. Firstly, we expanded the capabilities of double-sided auctions to handle a variety of program requests beyond a single quantity trade requests. Secondly, we developed flexible matching algorithms for double-sided auctions while ensuring the accuracy of an exchange's output. Lastly, we created a practical system for automatically detecting program violations that occurs when an exchange's output exceeds the validity bounds. To facilitate reproducibility of our research, all supporting materials including the formal proofs in Coq, verified code in OCaml and Haskell, as well as the demonstration video are available at https://danielfeitosa2.com/double-sided-auctions/. Additionally, the presentation slides can be found at https://danielfeitosa2.com/double-sided-auctions-slides/. Finally, our work was partially financially supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. Details regarding the awarded funds and project details can be found at https://danielfeitosa2.com/verified-event-stream-processing/.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for side observations.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, which leverages a short-term memory to temporarily store detector outputs and integrate them with the agent's current view in the environment.
The agent uses these combined representations to determine the optimal action through a contrastive loss.
By assessing various environment configurations, our experiments demonstrate that MemoNav outperforms leading agent-based methods by significant margins.
Additionally, our analysis shows that MemoNav's short-term memory's ability to incorporate side observations enhances navigation performance.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Building upon this, we introduce the idea of using Lie symmetry to develop predictive models for Krylov complexity as a function of energy, which we demonstrate for the SU(1,1) system. By comparing the ratios of direct decays versus breakup processes, the authors can determine the influence of $\alpha$-cluster correlations on the decay behaviors of the Hoyle state and its similarity to three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particle systems. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. This non-trivial characteristic may serve as the basis for implementing a quantum computation's anyon gate. Lastly, we calculated the critical magnetic field required for non-Abelian state formation, estimating this critical value for a purely s-wave superconducting phase to be approximately 1.5 times the critical field value in a purely Abelian system and 1.2 times the critical field value in a purely non-superconducting system. Conversely, we discovered that Rashba coupling's strength should be around 0.1 to 0.25 times the Planck and Dirac areas, as indicated by the ratio of coupling to bandwidth. Given that this coupling strength falls within the range that can be achieved with modern technology, our study presents a promising prospect for creating superconducting non-Abelian quantum computing devices.

Table facts play a key role in understanding data entries and forming concepts, yet identifying factual claims in unstructured forms remains unaddressed. This research is concerned with verifying factual claims related to tabular data, a format where facts are presented as structured sets of statements. To accomplish this, we define two essential tasks: Factual Consistency, which involves identifying if a claim is consistent with a table, and Factual Inference, which involves identifying if a claim can be logically inferred from a table. To test the effectiveness of these tasks, we created a set of table-based fact datasets, along with proposed models for addressing these tasks, and conducted experiments using these datasets. These experiments revealed that Negation Table Inference methods significantly enhance Factual Consistency performance, while Table Transformer methods deliver the best Factual Inference results. Yet, even with these models, there remains a significant gap in performance that can be attributed to the inherent ambiguities and negation table ambiguities present in these datasets. Despite this challenge, our proposed models achieve remarkable 85.65% Factual Consistency and 60.25% Factical Inference accuracy on our proposed datasets. In addition, we developed Pretrained Table Models, Pre-TM, which deliver 88.03% Factual Consistency and 64.35% Factical Inference accuracy on our proposed datasets. Interestingly, the difference in accuracy between these models and the state-of-the-art baselines is most pronounced for the Factual Inference task, especially when dealing with intrinsically challenging cases. This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. Additionally, we consider how these principles apply to other formal mathematical structures, exploring potential analogues in Quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we identify potential connections between the properties of complex numbers and the fundamental concepts of wavefunction interference and entanglement in Quantum mechanics. Lastly, we identify areas where the basic principles of complex numbers can be replaced by alternative mathematical structures, such as quaternions or complex forms of rational numbers, while exploring their implications for Quantum mechanics. This study is intended to provide an in-depth examination of the mathematical foundations of Quantum mechanics and their potential generalizations. Furthermore, it considers the potential application of its findings to other fields of study, such as Relativity and Bell's Theorem, and explores the implications of its findings for the broader field of physics. \end{abstract}

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. A new method of computing beta_k for all graphs using the first symmetric topological distance matrix row is presented, which works for any given k. While this method can be computationally expensive for large k, it allows for quick calculation of beta_k for small k values. Furthermore, it allows us to confirm previously proposed lower bounds on beta_k for certain graphs are, in fact, the minimum. Also, we too lower the minimum identifying set size for some graphs and show some graphs can't be pinpointed by any identifying set of size less than some number. Finally, an algorithm to quickly find the minimum identifying set in some graphs is presented. A new term "protocol" is also introduced to describe a sequence of numbers from these distance matrices. High numbers in these protocols are found to correspond to high beta_k values.   This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the

reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be constructed with

description of their differences. Additionally, we present a comprehensive case
study on predicting election outcomes based on opinion polls, highlighting the
advantages of using Indecision Trees over existing models. The proposed models and

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation. Although these approaches reduced time complexity, they lack guarantees and often fail for analogous reason - they may miss significant time series similarities. To address this, we introduced EAPrunedDTW, a DTW variant that not only terminates and omits DTW computations more intelligently, but also provides theoretical assurance for its efficacy. By comparing the proposed algorithm with EADTW and EDDTW, as well as EADTW*, on synthetic and real-world datasets, we observed that EAPrunedDTW outperforms these methods in terms of accuracy, while also achieving faster computation times - in some cases, even matching EADTW*'s precision without supplementary heuristic directions. Thus, we recommend EAPrunedDTW as an enhanced DTW algorithm for classification and clustering applications. Additionally, the proposed approach may serve as a potential foundation for further improvements in time series similarity search, potentially leading to more efficient and accurate time complexity and error bounds in this domain. The introduced algorithm also opens avenues for exploring more advanced pruning techniques, possibly enabling more precise and efficient time series analysis in the future. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide black-box test results, conveying whether a concept is correct through color-coded answers, or offer white-box explanations, revealing the step-by-step reasoning behind the assessment. Despite their benefits, both options have drawbacks: the simplified test results may lead to a lack of understanding of the correct solution, and the detailed explanations can be overwhelming for students. On the other hand, our proposed Testing Tutor seamlessly integrates these approaches by presenting various learning views that adapt to a student's performance. When initial results indicate a student needs more guidance, the tutor switches to providing white-box explanations; as the student demonstrates increasing understanding, the tutor gradually shifts to showing only the black-box test outcome. By utilizing concept-mapping, flowcharts, and natural deduction proofs as additional white-box explanation tools, the Testing Tutor offers a comprehensive learning experience that goes beyond simple test results. An exploratory study involving 32 first-year students who used the system as part of their database course revealed promising outcomes, including improved grades and increased student satisfaction. Specifically, while students who used traditional teaching methods performed poorly in the initial phase, ultimately achieving similar grades to those who used the system, the latter showed superior results when comparing pre-test and post-test scores. Moreover, a significant increase in student satisfaction was observed, as evidenced by survey responses. Subsequent case studies of five students who used the system revealed positive impacts of the inquiry-based learning approach, highlighting its potential to enhance both testing concepts and problem-solving skills. The findings suggest that the system can effectively support the learning of testing concepts, and our plans include conducting a study involving 50-60 students to further evaluate its efficacy in doing so. By doing so, we aim to enhance the reliability and transparency of machine learning solutions. To verify the efficacy of our method, we conducted comprehensive evaluations on two challenging breast cancer classification datasets. Our approach exhibited superior performance in highlighting relevant image regions, outperforming leading xAI methods. Our comprehensive axiomatic metrics analysis revealed that our technique excels in precision, coverage, and uniqueness, significantly surpassing the current state-of-the-art. Our findings suggest that visual phase-driven co-occurrence graphs are an effective solution for visually and interpretatively enhancing the reliability and transparency of deep learning-based solutions. The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the realm of cosmology, with predictions that can be tested through astronomical observations. The scenario in which an extra field remains unchanged during inflation is both the simplest implementation of the models and the most straightforward to model numerically. In this study, we have developed a numerical package, InflaPy, to calculate the spectral properties of perturbations produced by this model, taking into account situations in which the field's equilibrium state changes over time. The package's capabilities are demonstrated by calculating the spectral index and tensor-scalar ratio for a specific $\alpha$-attractor model, and by examining the distinct signatures that can result from the breakdown of equilibrium during inflation. In such cases, the predicted spectral properties are found to be concentration-dependent, giving rise to distributions rather than single values. The implications of this effect on determining the inflationary duration are also considered. The InflaPy package is designed to be user-friendly, with each calculation defined by a series of named functions that are described in the accompanying manual. The software is fully open-source and can be obtained at https://github.com/astrolabDT/InflaPy. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for academic purposes at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. In our analysis, we investigate how different approaches and domains influence acronym identification and disambigation performance using the F1-score metric. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of acronym context in disambigation through contextual analysis. Lastly, we discuss potential future research avenues and areas for improvement. Potential users of this system may submit their own domains by contacting the authors at amirv@uoregon.edu for personalized acronym glossary creation. Currently, the system supports acronyms in the scientific and biomedical domains; however, it can be easily extended to accommodate other domains upon request. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. While previous methods rely on inherently diverse primer pairs, our segment-identifying primers can be chosen with similar properties, enabling enhanced flexibility in the storage segment configuration. Additionally, we've developed enhanced algorithms for adding, updating and deleting data in the system, allowing for a more flexible and efficient DNA-storage solution. By introducing multiple tolerance thresholds for error correction, these algorithms reduce the amount of required DNA molecules and decrease the cost of writing operations. Our experimental results validate the effectiveness of this new strategy, and show that the proposed DNA-storage system can surpass the performance of existing DNA-storage methods in nearly all aspects. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. To further improve this method, we develop a learning-based refinement pipeline utilizing the predicted shapes, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in several image-based inverse problems on both synthetic and real datasets. Additionally, our approach supports simultaneous recovery of geometric deformations and underlying objects using self-supervision, showcasing promising results on synthetic and real datasets as well. Comprehensive evaluations through ablation studies and visualization analysis demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our proposed method. Furthermore, we provide the implementation details of our approach to ensure reproducibility and ease of adoption by the research community through an associated repository containing all necessary code and demo data. This repository can be accessed at https://github.com/ChengYang66/AccShade.

The framework utilizes a Markov process to analyze the probability of traffic states, represented by flow quantities, on individual links within a network. It's demonstrated that the variance in daily traffic flow can be broken down into three distinct components: a systematic trend, seasonal patterns, and randomly varying components. The probability distribution of daily flow is estimated using historical data, while considering the impact of systemic errors, measurement errors, and serial correlation. The proposed framework shows promising results in replicating the observed daily traffic patterns, including peak hours, seasonal variations, and unique characteristics such as "morning peak-midday valley-afternoon peak" patterns. Additionally, this framework offers a probabilistic analysis of daily traffic conditions, enabling the identification of unusual days and the probability of reaching critical thresholds in daily traffic volume. The proposed framework has potential applications in managing traffic and providing practical information for travelers and operational staff. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The observed agreement between the simplified model and the coupled oscillators' dynamics provides insight into the effective phase model's applicability in modeling global phase coherence in complex systems. The presented study is an expansion on previous work that initially explored phase coherence in conservative systems and has now been extended to include nonlinear coupling. The findings also discuss how the obtained phase, which is the order parameter in the system, relates to the oscillators' amplitude and how it differs from that obtained in other nonlinear systems where the frequencies are not random. The presented research may find application in modeling and understanding phase coherence in Josephson junction lattices and other materials with coupled nonlinear oscillators and varying frequencies. The obtained results could also be applied to manipulate a system exhibiting a similar phase in a quantum manner. By combining techniques, we've achieved an improvement in time complexity, obtaining an O(n^2) time efficiency, which surpasses the previous best of O(n^3) achieved separately by Brouder and Wilson. This new result is consistent with other known properties of the algorithms regarding node visits and degrees. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of adapting this result to obtain efficient algorithms for generating uniform random walks in more complex graphs, and this investigation leads to the discovery of a new property relating to the generation of random walks in p-regular graphs. Finally, we introduce a novel algorithm to efficiently generate random walks in p-regular graphs in O(n^2) time, and this result holds even in the case of sparse graphs with a regularity gap of theta(1/p). This new algorithm is consistent with the properties of the original random walks we just introduced. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis techniques and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise matching pairs of multimodal data. MusicTM-Dataset comprises three primary modalities: musical sheet audio, synthesized audio, and visual images – as well as accompanying text-based metadata. This dataset serves as a resource for developing methods bridging musical notation and audio or visual domains. To showcase the effectiveness of our dataset, a baseline strategy for cross-modal applications was implemented, achieving promising results in retrieval tasks. This research is open-source and the entire MusicTM-Dataset can be downloaded at https://github.com/dddzeng/MusicTM-Dataset. The code for our baseline experiment is available at https://github.com/dddzeng/MusicTM-Dataset/tree/main/cross_modal_retrieval. In the future, this dataset has the potential to support the development of more advanced methods featuring musical sheet, synthesized audio, and visual domains. Additionally, our research aims to introduce MusicTM-Dataset as a valuable tool for musical composition and generation applications. Currently, our research has presented a basic version of MusicTM-Dataset, which comprises approximately 77,000 sheets, 74,000 synthesized audio files, and 195,000 visual images. This dataset is continuously expanding to incorporate additional data from Music21, Musicsplit, and Music Information Retrieval tasks, including the development of musical composition and generation applications. Ultimately, our goal is to establish a comprehensive music dataset with an even broader scope of multimedia resources, facilitating the creation of more sophisticated music-related applications in the future. To this end, our research has presented a paper detailing the construction of MusicTM-Dataset at the ICME 2023 conference, and a companion paper outlining our research at the MM 2023 conference. Additionally, our team has developed an interface allowing users to access and explore MusicTM-Dataset, which can be accessed at https://www.musicTM.org. This project is sustained by regular updates with expanded content, and is positioned for continued growth as a premier music dataset. This knowledge will be shared in future research outputs. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration. Experimental findings demonstrate that this approach's effectiveness surpasses that of baseline methods. Moreover, the implementation's simplicity means it can be readily integrated into existing data visualization tools without requiring substantial technical knowledge. Overall, the proposed method's effectiveness in facilitating the exploration and discovery of Linked Data entities contributes to a more engaging user experience within Ontodia. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with substantial versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances the design of superconducting stellarators, enabling a range of rotational transform profiles. We demonstrate this through the revised design of the NRCDS stellarator, yielding a range of flexible designs. By optimizing the coil shapes using our approach, we achieved quasisymmetry accuracy better than 0.5% while allowing for a range of rotational transform values from 0.25 to 1.25. Furthermore, our design maintains a maximum module module magnitude below 0.12 and achieves an optimal filling factor greater than 0.92. We also investigate the stellarator's energy confinement properties using NCAR's MFC task force database. Our approach facilitates the exploration of stellarator design through analytical optimization, offering a range of design options that can serve as valuable references for research facilities. Ultimately, our design can contribute to optimizing Earth's magnetic field's rotational symmetry, which could impact space weather forecasting. Additionally, our design can inspire novel stellarator designs with built-in flexibility, paving the way for a new generation of versatile and quasisymmetric devices. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, as well as the possibility of integrating this method with concurrent MRI flow visualizations to investigate the reactor's optimal operating conditions.  Ultimately, this research could enable the development of model-free process models for catalytic reactors. The presented model could be employed for chemical engineering design and operational purposes.  The investigated reactor can be used for pharmaceutical synthesis on an industrial scale, and our temperature measurements will aid in optimizing the process.  The studied method can be applied for temperature measurements in various types of beds, such as fluidized beds, and will contribute to a better understanding of the chemical process at the reactor scale. The experimental variables that were changed were air flow rates of 50 and 100 cm per minute, with six experimental runs conducted in total. The measured temperature was found to have a linear relationship with water's proton resonance frequency in all conditions, with an average error of 1.5 degrees Celsius. The three-dimensional MRI temperature maps showed significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, with the temperature difference between the reactor's top and bottom sections quantified as 35 and 57 degrees Celsius for air flow rates of 50 and 100 cm per minute, respectively. The temperature variations observed were found to have an average error of 1.5 degrees Celsius when compared with optical temperature probe measurements. The study indicates the potential of combining MRI with proton NMR to investigate mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, as well as the possibility of using this technique to determine temperature distributions in various bed types, such as fluidized beds. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. The maximum number of different droplets in a mixture could be accurately predicted even without full knowledge of all interactions. The models' simulations confirmed these expectations and suggested the underlying rules for spatial organization through droplets could be widely applied across cellular molecular mixtures. The predictions made by these models were tested by creating a mixture of 50 different proteins and nucleic acids, which demonstrated the expected behavior. The results strongly supported the idea that droplet formation is a fundamental organizing principle in the cell. The principles of droplet formation could potentially be used to create new types of membraneless compartments with novel properties. The study's findings also opened up new avenues for studying self-assembly and organizing principles in complex systems. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC algebraic solvers compare in performance; and the influence of finite element grid size and structure on the BDDC method. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a cluster. Interestingly, the research found that BDDC outperforms AMG in most instances, with the largest speedup resulting from a comparison of methods for solving the heart's thick mass with 356,892 degrees of freedom, where BDDC exhibited a 5.5-to-6.5 times improvement over AMG. However, when modeling the heart's blood vessels using finely tuned grids with 67,852 degrees of freedom, BDDC showed only marginal gains over AMG, ranging from 10 percent to 50 percent faster. Ultimately, the research indicates that BDDC is more effective in solving cardiac mechanics problems, although the choice of solver remains dependent on the complexity of the problem. As a result, the use of BDDC is recommended for large-scale computations of heart mechanics on finite element grids. With the constant growth in capability to simulate complex, detailed heart anatomy, the research has the potential to improve patient-specific modeling and clinical applications, ultimately enhancing the precision of computer-modelled patient care. With the anticipated progression of simulating intricate heart structures, the research may one day enable the simulation of entire hearts, opening up new avenues for computer-modelled patient care. Moreover, the techniques employed in this research can be applied to the simulation of various other solid finite elasticity problems in medicine. For example, the models could be used in the simulation of brain surgery, while also contributing to the development of patient-specific surgical planning and the prediction of surgical outcomes. Furthermore, the research has the potential to improve surgical treatment decisions through computer simulation, ultimately facilitating surgical planning and predicting surgical results.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. In addition to providing a framework for evaluation, we also conducted an in-depth examination of common challenges and pitfalls in implementing lifelong learning methods, and through empirical studies, analyzed how different approaches perform in our custom-made environment. The full source code for L2Explorer is publicly available, and we encourage researchers to utilize our benchmark to promote consistent comparison and evaluation of lifelong learning methods. The intensity and diversity of these waves far exceed those found in Gevrey spaces as studied by Bourouni and Cote. Moreover, our research demonstrates that for any $s<3/2$, there exist travelling waves with arbitrarily large amplitudes and frequencies. Notably, our analysis shows that the regularity of these waves is tied to the parameter $s$, with more regular solutions emerging for lower values of $s$. The key to our findings lies in a new type of energy estimate, known as energy estimate with losses, which allows us to analyse irregular solutions and thereby expand the scope of our results. The analysis of these solutions is further complicated by our inability to accurately quantify their behaviour over very long time periods, which forces us to adopt an approach based on local time variations and adaptability. The discovery of these travelling waves highlights the complexity and irregularity of the 2D Euler equation, particularly in situations where solutions are smooth. The study also raises questions about the lower bound on the regularity of solutions that exhibit travelling wave behaviour, which could be significant in terms of the existing literature. Finally, our research is completed by a thorough discussion of various open questions and challenges. The most significant of these concerns the nature of solutions that exhibit rapid spatial oscillations and the possibility of developing a new theory of irregular solutions that is based on energy estimates with losses. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the imbalance by sampling difficult proposal counterparts from an off-the-shelf object detector, leading to a significant improvement in performance compared to the current state-of-the-art method. Our comprehensive evaluations demonstrate SABRA's effectiveness across multiple datasets and demonstrate its validity through analysis of the sampled proposals. Additionally, we address the challenge of negation proposal sampling by introducing a novel strategy based on clustering and balancing, which enhances the representation of difficult proposals and accelerates convergence during training. Our comprehensive experiments illustrate the advantages of this method and demonstrate improved accuracy on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO-TF datasets. Notably, our best model achieved an 8.2% improvement in average precision on the VRD task and demonstrated improved frequency-weighted average precision (FMAP) of 13.6%, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art method. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted via a series of repeated weak measurements. An experimental evaluation of this hypothesis is proposed using a two-qubit system consisting of an attenuated entanglement. Our findings are also extended to the context of weak measurements involving antitraces. Additionally, we introduce a generalized form of QCC applicable to a broader set of weak measurement procedures not justified by classical systems. Lastly, we demonstrate that this generalized QCC is directly related to the generalized TQD by a factor dependent on the weak measurement strength, with the difference between them only influenced by the positive operator-valued measure's overlap, potentially trivializing the discrepancy under specific conditions. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the quantum nature of weak measurement procedures. An open question is whether remaining quantum features can be extracted from a single weak measurement procedure. Our work also raises questions regarding the optimal strategy for extracting quantum correlation from weak measurements. An experimental approach to exploring these challenges is proposed. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in an open-source tool, integrated with the FloPoCo VHDL code generator, providing a complete flow from coefficients to hardware design. Thorough experiments were conducted to assess the models, followed by a detailed analysis of how design metrics impact actual hardware implementation. The findings are supported by numerous examples, including test cases, that are accessible online. Our software, supporting models, and corresponding test cases can be found at: https://github.com/qsystem3/MCM_ILP_optimization. Specifically, the ILP models can be found at: https://github.com/qsystem3/MCM_ILP_optimization/tree/main/ilp_models. Our approach achieved notable results in reducing the number of LUTs required to implement various MCM configurations, with improvements ranging from 10% to 40% compared to the current best practices. Furthermore, we identified an inherent drawback in our initial error propagation strategy and developed a possible amendment to address this issue in future research. Our work is expected to contribute to the creation of more efficient MCM hardware designs, paving the way for innovative applications in computing and digital signal processing. Finally, we recorded a notable improvement in area efficiency for all benchmark coefficients, with approximately 15% average reduction in LUTs, when intermediate precision was applied, compared to the full precision implementation. The average resource savings with intermediate precision led to approximately 5% average reduction in LUTs, while maintaining a specified error margin, compared to the single-precision approach. Our research indicates that accommodating intermediate precision in MCM designs can be advantageous, allowing for more resource-efficient hardware implementations while meeting application requirements for error tolerance. Our proposed approach demonstrates a strong correlation with actual hardware implementation, providing valuable insights into various design metrics. Our model's versatility enables support for multiple MCM configurations

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the pre-trained model's syntactic information to initialize self-attention weights in a linear projection matrix. While UPOA relies solely on this information, UPIO also incorporates additional constraints to maintain the bi-linear structure of self-attention weights, thereby enhancing its performance. Both models were evaluated on Splits 1 and 2 of the WSJ dataset and achieved satisfactory results, outperforming the baseline system in F-score by a significant margin. Furthermore, these models demonstrated the ability to learn relevant syntactic features from unstructured text, including sentence order, part-of-speech information, and branching patterns. Importantly, the proposed models demonstrated superior performance when combined with a weak supervision system using shallow parses, yielding substantial gains in F-score. Notably, the models' abilities to learn relevant features and achieve competitive performance in constituent parsing tasks were independent of their dependence on weak supervision. Finally, the proposed models were successfully applied to parsing tasks in low-resource settings, such as parsing German sentences using only English supervision, and also showed promising outcomes when parsing sentences in languages with limited resources and significantly different grammatical structures, such as parsing a sentence in Persian. Overall, the models achieved a reasonable F-score of 22.11. This research provides concrete evidence of the effectiveness of pre-trained models in unsupervised constituent parsing tasks, and also presents a viable solution for parsing tasks in low-resource settings. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into the advantages of employing HSI for object segmentation within complex urban settings. By leveraging the inherent properties of HSI, we overcome challenges posed by ambiguous scenes. Specifically, the paper presents a novel hyperspectral semantic segmentation model, demonstrating its efficacy through comparative evaluations on datasets mimicking cityscapes and remote sensing applications. The results reveal that the proposed approach surpasses its RGB counterpart and rival hyperspectral segmentation algorithms on multiple metrics. Moreover, the incorporated hyperspectral feature selection method streamlines computation, minimizing memory and processing efficiency. Consequently, the proposed model offers a streamlined solution for object segmentation in complex environments. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core rotation rate, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we explored possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a massive cloud of gas that slowed its core down or the presence of stellar non-sequence structures caused by a sudden and unexpected influx of mass from another star. Further observation and analysis are required to confirm whether this unusual phenomenon is a rare occurrence or a common internal structure of lower mass giant stars.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  We also developed a novel Bayesian RNN model, termed cRNN, to probe the importance of these auxiliary variables and perform category prediction.  By removing variables one by one and examining their impact on performance, we confirmed their significance and confirmed that auxiliary variables are essential for effective category prediction.  This study illustrates the capabilities of cRNN in dissecting hidden recurrent processes and highlights its potential for informing machine learning model design.  Additionally, cRNN can be applied in a wide range of scenarios beyond visual object categorization.  Ultimately, our research confirmed that auxiliary variables can be leveraged to enhance model performance in recurrent neural networks.  This understanding can be extended to other recurrent models beyond the specific case studied in this research. This value lies in the potential of cRNN to enhance our understanding of informed recurrence, which can lead to generalizable insights.  This potential value could be considered in existing research on recurrent neural networks, which has primarily focused on optimizing model performance. This research is unique in its approach, moving beyond existing methodologies that prioritize empirical testing of recurrent neural networks, which often examine various test cases, to instead focusing on understanding the underlying mechanisms that govern their informed recurrence. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. A particular method of studying these degrees involves analyzing the differential operators invariant under the group action. This analysis reveals new results in cohomology and provides a geometric interpretation of the transitivity degree. Additionally, this study confirms certain bounds on the transitivity degree, including bounds derived from the complexity of homogeneous spaces and toric varieties. Some of the key findings involve determining the transitivity degree for specific homogeneous spaces, such as Grassmannians, quadric surfaces, and hypersurfaces, while others involve establishing infinite transitivity degrees for certain homogeneous spaces and quasi-affine toric varieties. By combining invariant differential operators with a geometric interpretation of the transitivity degree, this study provides a new and powerful method of studying the transitivity degree in algebraic varieties. This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration. These theorems are constructed upon the foundation of previously published research articles by several authors. Additionally, we revise and refine some existing results, while also exploring novel applications of the main theorems. Specifically, we demonstrate the versatility of our theorems in addressing a range of closely related problems, such as those involving the case of one map that shares multiple hyperplanes with another, or when a meromorphic mapping shares multiple hypersurfaces with a nondegenerate map. Furthermore, we prove a unicity theorem for a special case of weakly analytic cyclic multiple function. Lastly, we finalize the paper by presenting several explicit examples that highlight specific scenarios in which the provided unicity theorems hold. These can be summarized as: for a complete Kähler manifold X with its meromorphic mapping f from X to CP^n and a nondegenerate map g from X to CP^n such that that f and g differ at a finite number of points in CP^n, if f and g share a specified number of hypersurfaces in CP^n, then f and g are actually the same mapping. These theorems, in turn, are founded upon a newly established general lemma, known as the key lemma, that allows us to analyze the behavior of meromorphic mappings between two complex manifolds under specific conditions. This key lemma enables us to directly apply it to a special case of weakly analytic cyclic multiple function, thereby simplifying our approach in comparison to previously published research. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained by applying ideal-theoretic operations to the polynomial system's algebraic locus. These operations typically involve symbolic pre-image computation and algebraic codimension assessment through related ideals theorema tertii type. For a specific codimension two system of polynomials, we demonstrate how the nondegenerate locus can be efficiently computed via numerical analysis, utilizing an algebraic variety decomposition method. This method leverages Lagrosa's variety decomposition algorithm to analyze an algebraic codimension assessment ideal. By differently interpreting the ideal as a codimension one system, the algorithm computes the nondegenerate locus. This approach has been implemented in the vardec package for the software Mathematica. Detailed results from testing are reported in the appendix. Additionally, a theoretical complexity assessment is provided in the discussion section. This involves computing the asymptotic complexity of the proposed method. In doing so, we introduce a novel problem-specific variant of the Partial Homology Class Computation problem, which we term Partial Homology Class Computation with a Filter. We then establish a lower bound on the expected running time of the proposed method. This work is, in part, a theoretical follow-up to our previous article on Lagrosa's variety decomposition algorithm. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new approach to study this problem and determine an asymptotic expression for the codegree squared sum of any 3-uniform hypergraph G, specifically the sum of the squares of its codegrees. Our novel idea for calculating this sum involves considering the expected codegree vector of a random 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices that avoids a given codegree vector. We demonstrate that this expected codegree vector is also a codegree vector, yielding an asymptotic expression for its squared sum. We derive several upper bounds for the Turan tetrahedron problem by manipulating this asymptotic expression, and our results include: a tight O(n^1/4) upper bound for the tetrahedron problem, and specific tight upper bounds for K42^3 and K43^3. We resolve the K41^3 problem by providing tight asymptotic upper and lower bounds, and we establish that the tetrahedron problem is likely to be statistically complete. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our modified version converges at a rate of O(h^2), surpassing the original method's O(h^p) performance (p > 2) and similar techniques. Furthermore, we present two singular system solvers for the complete Vandermonde matrix, one of which is an iterative algorithm. Implementing these techniques in periodical grid interpolation enables the preservation of the original method's monotonicity and convexity properties. Lastly, numerical experiments are conducted to validate our theoretical findings. When compared to the multiquadric based on the generalized Gaussian distribution, our proposed method provides greater accuracy, especially in the vicinity of the boundary. Additionally, it has been observed that the approximate eigenvalues of the complete Vandermonde matrix are remarkably close to 1, implying that the multiquadric may be efficiently minimized using the least squares method. However, this approach is hindered by the method's oscillatory behavior at periodic distances, demanding an alternative method for solving the least squares problem on the unit circle. Drawing inspiration from the Levinson-Durbin iteration, we adapt the method to obtain efficient solutions to the least squares problem while achieving stability and suppressing oscillations. Furthermore, it has been observed that our proposed method is more resilient to noise compared to the multiquadric. Taking this insight further, we develop two noisy data solvers for the complete Vandermonde matrix. Lastly, we present two noisy periodical grid interpolation techniques that preserve the original method's characteristics. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate our findings.
