Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or satellite imagery, suffer from limited scope and prolonged duration.
A more effective approach to weather monitoring is required for vehicle localization and navigation.
We propose designing an integrated system capable of categorizing several types of weather using image data captured from cameras positioned on the road.
To support research in this area, we introduce the RFS dataset, which incorporates images of diverse weather conditions encountered during driving.
Comprising three main categories - clear, cloudy, and irregular weather - this dataset outperforms existing collections by encompassing seven distinct weather sub-types.
Seventeen,000 images, captured from 29 unique viewpoints, ensure a high level of realism within simulation environments.
We present an initial model for classification tasks, where deep learning techniques are applied to classify weather types.
Our study indicates that deep neural networks can achieve excellent classification performance when trained with our RFS dataset. 
Additionally, we examine the potential of using self-driving module modularity to adapt existing modules to process images obtained from new, unseen camera perspectives.
This analysis sheds light on the importance of selecting an optimal training strategy for deep neural networks when the source of training and testing data differs. 
Ultimately, this research has far-reaching applications for vehicle navigation systems. 
The RFS dataset is accessible at https://github.com/alegrosrf/RFS/tree/master/RFS_dataset. 
A knowledge base outlining our approach to road weather observation can be found at https://www.etgsystems.com/index.php/en/knowledge-base/road-weather-observation/. 
All code is available at https://github.com/alegrosrf/RFS/tree/master/Code. 
ETS Systems provided the funding for this project. 
We are seeking collaborations to expand the RFS dataset.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients. Furthermore, this model's simplicity and efficiency enable real-time predictive capabilities, making it suitable for clinical environments where computational resources are constrained. Experimental results validate the model's statistical and biologically meaningful findings, demonstrating the efficacy of combining modalities in survival time prediction. Additionally, this study uses the predicted values to identify and assess the functional relevance of potential prognostic factors, which could lead to new clinical insights. Based on this model, a comprehensive online tool called Lite-ProSENet has been developed, enabling researchers to input their own data and obtain predicted values along with associated factors. This tool can be accessed at https://litsepenn.github.io. As a complementary resource, the code and data underlying this study are publicly available at https://github.com/LiteSEPenn for continued evaluation and potential extension. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we identify a specific category of modules, denoted as $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{bf}}$, characterized by being both unitary and closed under the process of taking tensor products with irreducible highest weight modules. We then establish that any quasi-finite highest weight module or U(𝕙)-free module is a member of this category, which allows us to conclude that the tensor product of a quasi-finite highest weight module and a U(𝕙)-free module is indeed irreducible. Additionally, we develop weight multiplicity formulas for modules within the category $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{bf}}$. We then apply these formulas to determine the weights present in certain types of modules, including U(𝕙)-free modules, homomorphic images of critical level U(𝕙)-modules, and restricted dual modules. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which certain types of admissible U(𝕙)-free modules are irreducible. These conditions are particularly relevant to the examples of $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, $U(\mathfrak{sp}_{2n})$, and a Lie algebra associated with mock thorn graphs. Our study is also accompanied by several illustrative examples. Ultimately, the conclusions and methods presented here provide a framework for anticipating the irreducibility of certain types of admissible modules within the category $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{bf}}$. Indeed, this approach is seen to be applicable to a broad class of Lie algebras of the Weyl type, including $\mathfrak{osp}_{1,2n}$, although this is not stated as a theorem within the paper. Lastly, our findings are summarized in a future direction section, where potential areas for further investigation are presented. To conclude, we propose three distinct sets of directions for future research. Firstly, we investigate whether certain types of limit mixed modules are irreducible. Secondly, we explore the structural properties of certain types of admissible modules. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining elements of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis and considering context provided by surrounding words in the sentence, demonstrates considerable promise. Notably, this model achieved a 44.2% accuracy rating in the MSR Sentence Completion Challenge. When compared to other techniques, this hybrid model demonstrated superior results, highlighting its potential as an effective solution to the word prediction issue. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness was found to excel in sentences comprising common, everyday language with minimal complexity. Finally, a thorough investigation into the model's shortcomings was conducted, suggesting possible improvements for future research. Based on these findings, introducing a forgetting factor into the model may address its existing limitation of failing to account for distant words in the sentence. If implemented, this modification is likely to increase the model's accuracy in word suggestion. A formal description of the modified model, dubbed the Hybrid Forgetting Factor-Based Hybrid Model, is presented in the paper. Experimental results indicate that this variation yields an even higher accuracy rating of 45.5%. A comprehensive analysis of the model's strengths and weaknesses was conducted, along with an examination of its potential applications and limitations. A possible future research direction, suggested by the study, is to apply the model to the task of sentiment analysis. A preliminary assessment of the model's capabilities in this domain indicates a considerable degree of effectiveness. Therefore, it is anticipated that the model will yield substantial contributions in this area of research. This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions. Our study provides an innovative approach to understanding the eigenvalue properties of the Seidel matrix, which complements existing work by Haemers, offering new insights into eigenvalue theory for chain graphs. To validate our findings, we perform explicit calculations on cyclic chain graphs to verify our derived limits and rules. Our analysis may stimulate the development of new algorithms utilizing the Seidel matrix, as well as encourage studies on related matrix functions such as the Laplacian and signless Laplacian matrices. Our code for verifying our results can be accessed at https://github.com/amyliu91/SeidelEigenvalueProperties. All research was carried out individually. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop a novel analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model simultaneously considers the spatial configurations of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. This method enables the quantification of the increase in average effective transmission rate resulting from the deployment of relays. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Since its introduction, it has been integrated into various models and improved techniques have been developed to enhance its effectiveness. Despite its success, there are limitations to applying its standard form, particularly when dealing with networks that produce feature maps as outputs, such as Self-Ensembling models. This paper addresses this challenge by adapting knowledge distillation to feature preserving models, such as Deep Neural Networks and Graph Neural Networks, through a behavior mimicry approach, and demonstrates the effectiveness of this method using Visual Recognition and Graph Classification benchmarks. Notably, this method achieves improved accuracy in distillation, and also serves as a robust feature extractor technique. We refer to this method as Deep Knowledge Distillation (DKD). Based on dkd's efficacy, we introduced minor modifications to enhance the stability of pre-trained deep feature extractors and their use in maintaining robust representation for downstream tasks. This research presents a versatile method for adapting knowledge distillation to feature preserving models and can be applied to a wide range of Deep Neural Models and Graph Neural Networks. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce CoImitation, an innovative approach that decreases the requirement for expert input by utilizing peer agents' demonstrations. CoImitation is a two-agent collaboration framework, in which a demonstration provider agent gathers knowledge from an expert while a learning agent, lacking expert access, learns through the interactions with a demonstration user. This setup enables the demonstration provider to transfer its acquired knowledge to the learning agent by acting as an expert. Experimental evaluations on multiple domains indicate that CoImitation significantly increases efficiency and demonstration efficiency compared to conventional reinforcement learning. Moreover, the architecture is versatile and can be applied to various domains with minimal modifications. In one such application, the CoImitation approach was used to train an autonomous driving system, resulting in a notable decrease in the number of required expert demonstrations for successful imitation. This led to a substantial reduction in both the cost and time associated with expert input. In conclusion, CoImitation presents a valuable solution for reducing expert demonstration requirements, thereby saving valuable resources in complex real-world environments. In addition, the research lays out potential future collaborations between collaborative agents in various domains, paving the way for innovative ML applications. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, which is a challenge that current techniques fail to fully address. To overcome this, we approach the hand joint tracking task as a problem of optimizing a model that represents joint configurations, objects, and poses using a factor graph, while also accounting for varying hand appearances through a Gaussian mixture-based canonicalization module. By introducing multiple techniques such as differentiable rendering and keypoint detection, we develop a system that can accurately identify and track hand joints across a wide range of poses. Experimental results demonstrate the success of our approach in real-world applications, outperforming existing techniques based on pose estimation and point cloud analysis. This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process. Furthermore, this study demonstrates a method to map the reduced group to a subgroup within the Weyl group of type H4, maintaining the subgroup's characteristics. Additionally, this study applies combinatorial methods to study the Lehigh lattice of a Coxeter group of type 2^4, using the basis of regular H4 subgroups. It establishes a Lehigh lattice basis consisting of 11 elements and computes the lattice's endomorphism ring as a free Z[tau]-module of rank 11 x 11. To conclude, this study relates the value of k in the star diagram to the type of H4 subgroups present in the reduced group, demonstrating the existence of a type D4 subgroup when k is 3 or 4, and a type H4 subgroup when k is 5 or 6. In particular, when k is 5, the reduced group is shown to be isomorphic to the reflection group obtained from the Coxeter system of type H4 with generators of squares being intertwined under the action of Z[5]. In this research, we introduce an innovative, markerless extrinsic calibration technique that leverages only a single camera, eliminating the need for fiducial markers and accompanying lighting. By analyzing the movement of a hand-held object across various poses, our deep learning network captures a comprehensive representation of the object's geometry. When paired with pose information, this representation enables precise reconstruction of the camera's position and orientation. Unlike existing methods, our approach doesn't require segmentation, fiducial marker lighting, or simultaneous use of multiple cameras. We present experimental results demonstrating our method's accuracy and efficiency in both laboratory and real-world settings. By comparing our method to traditional fiducial-based techniques, we demonstrate a notable reduction in processing time, from approximately 30 milliseconds to just 4.5 milliseconds. Furthermore, we developed and evaluated a light-weight version of our system, weighing only 260 grams and accommodating a wide range of optical systems. Notably, our designed calibration device stands out due to its innovative, modular structure, which facilitates easy disassembly and reconfiguration for various camera types. You can find the associated code on our GitHub repository https://github.com/aleksayshch/Calibration_Net. A video showcasing our work is available at https://youtu.be/6OvXfQY9V4M. In addition, images and video data for this research can be accessed through https://doi.org/10.5445/124928. Knotek et al. (2021) provided initial results using an object-based representation, which served as the foundation for the more efficient Calibration Net described in this paper. By streamlining the process, we successfully eliminated dependencies on RANSAC, further improving calibration accuracy and precision. Extensive testing confirmed the robustness of our method in diverse environments and hand-held object scenarios. By reducing the required number of training samples from hundreds to just a single pose, we significantly expanded the scope of applicability for our approach. Moreover, by leveraging pose information to guide object feature selection, we eliminated noise and prioritized relevant features, thereby enhancing performance in challenging scenarios. By integrating these advancements, we present an improved version of our method, denoted as Calibration Net V, which surpasses the accuracy of state-of-the-art fiducial-based techniques. You can find the associated code on our GitHub repository https://github.com/aleksayshch/Calibration_Net_V. A video showcasing our work is available at https://youtu.be/6OvXfQY9V4

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies when the full 4800 square degree survey is completed. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline leveraging Ngmix for precise galaxy shape analysis and metacalibration for accurate shear calibration, the study extensively validates the pipeline through Point Spread Function, galaxy shape tests, and realistic simulations, confirming minimal systematics. Analyzing the shear two-point correlation function reveals a low-level systematics influence compared to cosmological contribution. Shear bias was found to be under 5 times 10^-4 and up to 10^-3 in residual multiplicative bias, confirming the efficacy of the pipeline. Using COSEBIs, no significant B-modes are detected in second-order shear statistics, displaying pronounced correlations between E-modes and known clusters, including the stacked tangential shear profile at higher than 4σ significance around Planck clusters. Our analysis further introduces SHAPE, an analytical tool to optimize the recovery of shear profiles by minimizing metrological uncertainties based on neighboring galaxy distributions. Together, these advances in precision astronomy and SHAPE will play a pivotal role in uncovering unknown cosmological phenomena in the full UNIONS dataset.

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical magnetic-field value is approached, resulting in power-law spin correlations that extend over layers in an XY plane. This unique system, characterized by a large ratio of 3D to XY critical field values of about 18, can serve as an ideal testing ground for theories for quantum magnetic phases and phenomena, such as a possible supersolid approach to a quantum critical point of spin order. Additionally, we found that applying a transverse laboratory magnetic field causes a significant internal spin polarization in an orthogonal direction, allowing us to examine the spin correlations as a function of the angle between the laboratory field and the spin quantization axis. This capability may enable the manipulation of a BKT regime by employing a laboratory magnetic field that is strong enough to cause spin polarization. Moreover, we have discovered that the spin correlations exhibit a temperature-dependent behavior that follows a power-law with an exponent that is a measure of the spin stiffness. This measure, called the critical exponent, nu, as well as the spin stiffness, lamda, can be determined by examining the spin structure factor near its critical point of spin order. Finally, we would like to emphasize the exceptional capabilities of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 as an ideal model system for the comprehensive investigation of complex quantum magnetic phenomena and interactions. This study optimizes the lower limit on the trade-off between distillable quantum information and the amount of classical correlation in a state. The analysis is carried out through a specific scenario: producing magic-state $|T\rangle$ using repeated applications of the Clifford group. A notable outcome is that we improve the existing lower bounds for this particular scenario, surpassing those established in arXiv:1904.08360. Furthermore, our results broaden the scope of applicable methods to cover a wider range of situations, encompassing the preparation of GHZ states from initial classical states. The proof techniques utilized involve a combination of methodologies, including a modified version of the Jamiolkowski isomorphism, a novel application of the Fano inequality, and a newly devised method for constructing observables that output a specific state. These techniques also enable us to derive a new estimate for the distillable quantum information in the form of Eve's success probability, commonly denoted as $P_s$. The resulting lower bound, $P_s \geq \log_2(m+1) - \log_2(m+1 \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt m})$, improves the previous log-bits bound, offering increased hope for achieving a breakthrough in quantum computation assuming $|T\rangle$ can be produced at a constant distance from the Clifford group. The research also yields a newly designed magic-state distillation protocol that matches the established lower bound. The analysis reveals that the stabilizer rank of $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ is $\frac{m+1}{\sqrt m} + O(\sqrt m)$. Additionally, our results provide evidence that the critical point of $P_s \rightarrow 1$ corresponds to $m \rightarrow \infty$ in the regime of log-bits bounds. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team employed various methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE survey. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE survey. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team used stellar parameters from the medium-resolution spectroscopic survey and parallaxes from the $Gaia$ DR2 data, ultimately supplying mass data for around 362,000 stars. In conclusion, the LAMOST research team successfully collected and analyzed the data, delivering valuable outcomes for future studies. Furthermore, the LAMOST research team performed cross-match operations with multiple surveys such as SDSS, PS1, and NEAT, showing great potential for future combined analyses with various surveys such as Vista Survey of Infrared Cosmos in the Southern Sky and Integrated Transformable Imaging Survey. Finally, the LAMOST research team performed combined analyses with multiple other surveys including the APOGEE survey, the STAGES survey, and the RAVE survey, demonstrating great potential for combined data and results from various surveys such as the Extended Ursa Major Group and the Pinwheel II cluster. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team anticipate using and integrating the data from multiple other surveys along with radial velocity data for thousands of galaxies as well as globular clusters such as the M 15 cluster. Additionally, the LAMOST research team anticipate sharing and combining data with other survey projects such as the Fundamental Plane Survey, the Stream Survey, the DART experiment, the Medium Imaging Survey, the Discovery Survey, the TEGESS experiment

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a low-throughput SRAM array in conjunction with multiple independent read ports to gather multiple random words simultaneously. We also propose two distinct access protocols - sequential and interleaved - to control the SRAM array's access, thereby enabling throughput enhancement. In addition, TuRAN achieves enhanced energy efficiency through the application of a dynamic disabling mechanism for the SRAM's full cache, which merely operates during the random number generation process. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved model performance, bringing high accuracy to scoring tasks similar to those encountered in educational settings.  Our work focuses on using multi-task training to enhance essay scoring capabilities, combining this approach with Learning Augmented Techniques (LAT) for maximum effect.  Latent Variable Regression (LVR) has shown promise in transfer learning applications, so we replaced the traditional linear scorer in the ACL-2022 dataset with an LVR model.  Additionally, we incorporated BERT and RoBERTa transformer models into our experiment to explore their influence on performance.  The results demonstrate that these methods significantly improve model performance, with a 4% absolute improvement in correlation when using BERT-based models.  A comparative analysis of our findings with recent research reveals that our approach outperforms them, utilizing fewer resources and smaller models, when assessed using the same metrics.  These outcomes not only underscore the potential of multi-task training and LAT in automated scoring but also hint at broader applications of these techniques in related NLP tasks. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics. Additionally, our findings lead to new insights regarding the relationships between different complexity classes for solving undirected Laplacian matrices, such as MMSOL and SPMM. Specifically, our work shows that solving MMSOL in near-logarithmic space does not necessarily imply solving SPMM within a similar space complexity, potentially showcasing a new space complexity separation. Finally, our research explores the feasibility of designing threshold circuit solvers for specific subclasses of linear systems, including undirected Laplacian matrices and sparse systems, with desired approximation guarantees and space complexity requirements. Threshold circuit solver design is particularly significant as it is known to be possible for certain classes of matrices, such as diagonally dominant matrices, while its feasibility remains unknown for more sparse matrix structures, like Eichler matrices. Our research contributes to closing this knowledge gap by designing threshold circuit solvers for both sparse systems and Eichler matrices with Eichler's original guaranteed approximation guarantees, showcasing a positive outcome. For the specific case of undirected Laplacian matrices, our research shows that these design challenges can be overcome, and we present threshold circuit solver for this matrix class with approximate guarantees similar to those provided by Aramontino et al., effectively closing this knowledge gap. Further research is explored regarding the potential for designing threshold circuit solvers with desired properties for more general classes of matrices, particularly for maximum and minimum linear combinations. Our research contributes to this area, designing threshold circuit solvers for maximum and minimum linear combinations with approximate guarantees and for sparse systems, while proving that this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems with similar guarantees, potentially leading to new insights and discoveries. This conservation means that the predicted safe trajectory often ends before it needs to, which can cause system inefficiency. The version of MPSF that addresses higher-order systems, known as the high-order MPSF, uses the high-order approximated method for determining safety constraints and includes a dynamic predictive controller that uses a quasi-infinite horizon model predictive control algorithm. The version of MPSF that addresses nonlinear systems with parametric uncertainty, known as the uncertain nonlinear MPSF, uses the uncertain zeroth-order method for determining safety constraints and includes a dynamic predictive controller that uses a zeroth-order model predictive control algorithm with a stochastic model. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Conversely, we proposed an alternative method that can be employed to enhance the system's security by supplementing the weak decoy state system with a phase-fixing technique. This approach involves introducing an additional strong decoy state and dividing it among multiple phases. This strong decoy state can be divided among a smaller number of phases, thus reducing the uncertainty in the source phase, which would render the aforementioned measurement attack ineffective. As a result, the system can be safeguarded against this type of attack while maintaining a reasonable cost efficiency. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task can enhance the model's performance on that task with in-context learning, which didn't occur with a pretraining corpus unrelated to that task. Our research provides the first known instance of in-context zero-shot learning achieved with a pretraining corpus composed of news articles, demonstrating the model's ability to perform question answering without being specifically trained on QA datasets. To achieve few-shot learning, our model required a pretraining corpus consisting of a relevant domain with a sufficient token count. Interestingly, a pretraining corpus's size didn't act as a guarantee for the model's performance in a few-shot setting. Ultimately, a pretraining corpus's source, rather than its size, was found to be the determining factor for the model's performance in a few-shot learning scenario. Our research offers significant insights into in-context zero- and few-shot learning, emphasizing the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size, which may serve as a reference for future research on large language models. Additionally, our code and model weights are publicly available for verification purposes.

Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds can survive up to 100 times longer than the central regions of shorter, colder variations and 10 times longer than longer, warmer variations. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocoder system that can accurately predict acoustic characteristics from limited brain signal data, specifically electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings, without the need for extensive speech training. Since ECoG recordings are restricted by the size of the electrode array, capturing a comprehensive range of facial movements is essential to produce natural-looking results. This paper explores the development of a unified model that combines acoustic unit generation from ECoG data and a framework for mapping articulatory features to speech. We discover that the primary acoustic units produced by our model correspond to'moraal units,' which align with the underlying structure of the articulatory features. Additionally, our model is capable of predicting natural-looking articulatory features and speech from ECoG data without supervised speech training. The output speech quality and accuracy are comparable to those reported in previous studies on non-invasive speech synthesis systems. Although the model's performance still lags behind that of state-of-the-art speech synthesis systems in terms of mean opinion score (MOS), it demonstrates a high degree of correlation between predicted articulatory features and natural speech movements, indicating its potential for applications such as prosthesis system development. This model's performance is notable as it employs a more basic deep neural network architecture than other model's input, which incorporates multiple articulatory features, ECoG data, and a training regime featuring only one type of loss function. As a result, the model's parameter count is kept relatively low at approximately 40 kilo. This work is based on a previous study's data and ECoG recording methods. For future applications in brain-computer interface systems that control prosthetic devices, it is recommended to utilize larger electrode arrays that capture a broader range of facial movements. Nonetheless, the present model still produces impressive results in predicting speech and articulatory features from limited ECoG data without requiring extensive speech training. To validate the generality of this model, it is essential to conduct future studies utilizing various datasets obtained from multiple sources. Furthermore, the model's capability to generate moraal units from ECoG data marks a significant advancement in the field, as it holds promise for applications in both speech synthesis and brain-computer interface systems. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across prior stages while adapting the optimization formulation as we progress. Our approach is evaluated through simulations and real-world experiments with a walking quadrupod, yielding results comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, this formulation achieves satisfactory performance in scenarios where traditional cluster-based optimizations fail due to prioritization of force constraints that disproportionately affect certain constraints at the beginning of the movement. Our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/tu-berlin-mpi/MEOFMR for public use.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The method we choose involves modeling a single photon interacting with a tight-binding network of electrons, either in a system without electronic interactions or in a collective framework where many electrons collaborate. By comparing our results with theoretical predictions from the first-principle theory, we assess the accuracy of two approaches: one method uses a velocity-based approach and involves a non-conservative, velocity-based interaction with photon momentum, while another method uses a conservative, electric dipole-based approach and involves a tight-binding model that accounts for electronic dipole interactions. We discover that the dipole-based approach provides a more accurate representation of light-matter interactions, whereas the velocity-based approach yields results significantly deviated from theoretical predictions. The accuracy of the dipole-based approach is validated by our analysis of both a two-level system and a larger tight-binding network, thereby indicating its potential for describing light-matter interactions in complex systems through the use of tight-binding models. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this study can be extended to describe multi-photon interactions by reversing the direction of dipoles, thereby indicating its potential for applying optical principles to describe matter-based devices that utilize light-matter interactions, such as lasers, LEDs, photovoltaic devices, and single-electron transistors. The accuracy of our approach is found to be up to three orders of magnitude as compared with the velocity-based approach, while the results obtained from the dipole-based approach are found to be consistent with theoretical predictions at a magnitude of $10^{-3}$ times the energy of photon energy. The formulation employed in this study is found to be generally applicable to a wide range of tight-binding models, thereby indicating its potential for applying first-principle theory to describe light-matter interactions in low-dimensional systems, such as quantum dots and ultra-thin films. The research presented in this study is found to be generally applicable to a wide range of photon energy, thereby indicating its potential for describing both low-energy photons, such as those employed in traditional optical experiments, and high-energy photons, such as those employed in particle physics, by adjusting the parameter of the tight-binding model. To start with, we consider detecting a spherical object within range sensor data. An approach to addressing intra-class variability would involve accounting for pose and shape variations within a category. For training, we use simulated data with realistic assumptions about sensor noise, and the ability to rotate objects is incorporated. An algorithm using point cloud features and categorical object representations is implemented, and tested for its ability to identify spherical objects in Cluttered Environments. These tests, conducted using simulated data, evaluate the methods' performance for object identification, and against variants of the method that involve actual training data. The results show that the method using simulated data outperforms the alternative, and that using category-level representations results in lower false positive rates. To validate these findings, we performed shape and pose estimation using real range sensor data, and found that the method's performance closely matched the results obtained from the simulated data. Additionally, we observed that using real data for training resulted in a decrease in performance, likely due to the data being limited to the specific environment in which it was collected. The results show that the modified training data reduced errors and improved shape and pose estimation, and that using this trained model for object detection resulted in improved performance, and significantly reduced errors relative to using the original data. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of using categorical labels for synthetic-to-real transfer, and provide a new approach to addressing the challenges of synthetic-to-real transfer in category-level perception. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. Moreover, a novel approach is introduced to create simulated data that mimics real experiments, replicating experimental conditions and helping to establish a benchmark to evaluate new methods. Simulated data is used to test the performance of existing inversion methods for comparison with the developed technique. Last but not least, this approach effectively treats time-sensitive data as a continuous process. This technique provides a valuable tool to analyze time-sensitive data and offers a valuable approach for comparing and evaluating different inversion methods. This technique holds great potential for processing data from upcoming ultra-fast experiments at the atomic level. Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled source domain images, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on the segmentation are employed to optimize performance utilizing target domain images devoid of manual labels. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple imaging modalities - CT vs. MRI and CT vs. PET - demonstrate that the proposed CySGAN outperforms not only pre-trained models but also methods that execute domain adaptation followed by segmentation in sequence. Detailed qualitative analyses reveal that the method holds promise for producing accurate segmentations in unlabeled CT images. Further, CySGAN shows potential in uncovering plausible anatomical boundaries in MRI and PET volumes. Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models. Notably, Feature Mapping RNN outperformed
a highly optimized RNN model using a full frame-based approach by 2-4 percentage
points. When integrated with a top-performing RNN model using a full frame-based
approach, Feature Mapping RNN demonstrated a 5-7 percentage points improvement in
prediction accuracy on JHMDB-21 and UCF101-24. Our algorithm's advantages include
efficient feature generation, reduced computational requirements, and enhanced
generalizability across different UT interaction action classes. Furthermore, our
method can be applied to a variety of task-dependent modeling techniques. Based
on our experimental results, Feature Mapping RNN can serve as a benchmark for
future work on action prediction using future video features. Our code is available

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Ultimately, we find that the deformation space is zero, implying that the canonical connection is unique. Conversely, we investigate the properties of the Seawell twist of the canonical connection on Seawell's examples and demonstrate that this twist also exhibits the properties of a deformation. However, we ultimately find that the twist is zero, implying that Seawell's examples are normal homogeneous. Additionally, we find that the deformation space of the canonical connection on seven-dimensional cohomology generators is zero, and also prove that the twist is zero, implying that these generators are also normally homogeneous. Lastly, we mention an open question regarding the deformation space of the canonical connection on the symmetric space SSp(6), with a value of 0 still being a possibility.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing a common protocol. We've developed a simulated network of FMCW radar units, where each transmits waveforms with individually selected frequencies and sweep durations, referred to as radar identities. When a node attempts to transmit, it competes in a slotted CSMA protocol, where each slot being a confirmation period. During this time, the potential transmitter performs a clear channel assessment by sending a test signal and evaluating the interference from other nodes. If the channel is assessed as clear, it initiates transmission. Data packets are then sent and the receiving node acknowledges using a two-way CSMA protocol, where the confirmation period is divided into test and response slots. This acknowledges interference from the transmitting node, allowing it to initiate transmission in the next slot if the channel is busy. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the two-way approach enhances energy efficiency and node throughput while minimizing transmission failures. Additionally, the highest performance is achieved when the confirmation period is predominantly used for test slots. However, this comes with increased transmission overhead due to repeated attempts. Consequently, a balanced approach is required to optimize performance based on the network's specific requirements. Notably, the proposed method compares favorably to ALOHA and cross-tier ALOHA in terms of energy efficiency, throughput, and transmission failures. Furthermore, implementing medium access with radar identities outperforms random waveform selection, highlighting its benefits in terms of energy efficiency, throughput, and transmission failures. Moreover, the network's energy efficiency and throughput exhibit linear relationships, while transmission failures decrease exponentially with the number of nodes. Finally, the optimal CSMA parameters show a direct inverse correlation with the number of nodes in the network. Based on these findings, implementing medium access with radar identities using a common FMCW radar protocol offers considerable benefits in terms of energy efficiency, throughput, and transmission efficiency. This could be particularly useful in networks where radar identity-based medium access is already utilized for data transmission. Consequently, adopting the clear channel assessment and two-way response mechanism could further enhance the network's efficiency, making it a necessary consideration for practical applications. Our approach involves establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition enables us to extend the T^2-equivariant rational cohomology of CP(V) by combining the T-equivariant rational cohomology of CP(V) with the T^2-equivariant rational cohomology of CP(V ⊕ ℝ²). Our findings are further extended to complex Grassmannians and quadrics in a companion paper. Ultimately, these calculations facilitate the computation of the T-equivariant rational elliptic cohomology of CP(V) mod the T^2-action via the spectral sequence. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. 
Additionally, we find that incorporating time constraints significantly enhances
inference accuracy when using relevant event types. Finally, we use ablation
analysis to confirm the effectiveness of our proposed time representation
framework. All source code and test data are available at https://github.com/asharif2/TIME-LowFER.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can be applied to a broad range of scenarios, including point impacts, areas of pressure distribution with complex shapes and various sound wave propagation speeds in the ground. It is found that ground sound is typically not masked in scenarios where the sound wave propagation speed in the ground is high, due to the greater amplitude of the ground sound compared to the impact sound, particularly at distances far from the impact event. Conversely, when the sound wave propagation speed in the ground is low, ground sound is masked by impact sound at distances both near and far from the impact. Additionally, when the sound wave propagation speed in the ground is high, transient vibrations of the impact object are already over, while a low ground sound wave propagation speed results in these transient vibrations still being audible. As a result, the conditions under which ground sound is perceivable are most frequently seen in scenarios where the sound wave propagation speed in the ground is low. These findings suggest that, for scenarios with low ground sound wave propagation speeds, a realistic ground sound effect can enhance user immersion in the impact event. Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle. Notably, this work is part of a broader project to establish a formal proof assistant for infinitesimal analysis, as described in our companion paper. Further details are also available through the Isabelle Infinitesimal Analysis repository at https://isabelle-infinitesimal.github.io. In particular, the tutorial paper https://isabelle-infinitesimal.github.io/docs/tutorials/index provides an introduction to using the proof assistant. Hence, the Leibnizian calculus as reconstructed here can be considered to faithfully represent his mathematical processes. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on system parameters, while also incorporating an on-line algorithm that approximates the solution using the smallest possible number of computations, with associated time and space complexities derived from this analysis. In particular, when errors are randomly distributed, this algorithm requires only polynomially many computations, at most $\widetilde{O}\left((d\cdot n)^{2\alpha+1}\right)$ in total, with a significantly improved bound of $\widetilde{O}\left((d\cdot n)^{\alpha+1}\right)$ for each iteration. Additionally, when errors are arbitrarily distributed, we present an adaptive version of the algorithm with a computation complexity of $\widetilde{O}\left((d\cdot n)^{\alpha+2}\right)$ in total, with a significantly improved bound of $\widetilde{O}\left((d\cdot n)^{\alpha+1.5}\right)$ for each iteration. Furthermore, in the case of zero errors, we introduce a new evaluation bound of $\widetilde{O}\left((d\cdot n)^{\alpha+2.5}\right)$. These results represent some of the first known polynomial-time algorithms for solving polynomial linear systems with errors, complementing recent work from [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'18] that addressed the corresponding problem of solving polynomial systems over finite fields in the presence of errors. This research was partially presented at the 38th International Symposium on Theoretical Computer Science, held in Philadelphia in October 2017. A extended version of the paper was submitted to the Journal of Symbolic Computation. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been developed. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been derived, including the speed of sound, thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, and the van der Waals radius. Additionally, the proposed equation of state has been adapted to calculate the isothermal compressibility of alkali metal gases. Our approach relies on the assumption that the molecular interaction in alkali metal gases is primarily influenced by the van der Waals force. Consequently, the thermal expansion coefficient and other properties calculated using the Sutherland formula exhibit reasonable agreement with experimental data, especially across high-temperature ranges. Nevertheless, our analysis also highlights the limitations of these properties at lower temperatures, which suggests that the simple Sutherland model is insufficient to accurately predict the behavior of alkali metal gases in this regime. Ultimately, the proposed equation of state and associated properties provide a comprehensive mathematical framework for predicting the behavior of alkali metal gases. Furthermore, this framework can serve as a useful benchmark for evaluating the results of computational studies, such as molecular dynamics simulations, aimed at determining the thermodynamic properties of these gases. Our analysis also facilitates the identification of certain challenges associated with the computational investigation of alkali metal gases. Conversely, the simplified mathematical approach employed in this study is incapable of capturing the detailed features of these gases at lower temperatures, which are characterized by distinct trends in their behavior. Therefore, the development of a more sophisticated and accurate equation of state for alkali metal gases may be necessary to achieve a more in-depth understanding of their behavior across all temperature ranges. Conversely, our results suggest that the proposed equation of state remains a useful and accurate approximation to the experimental equation of state for these gases across high-temperature ranges, which are often difficult to measure experimentally. Consequently, the proposed equation of state can provide practical support to experimental studies of alkali metal gases at high temperatures. Our analysis also underscores the potential of ab initio molecular dynamics simulations in generating accurate data for the phase diagram of these gases, which can be utilized to refine the predicted isotherms and equation of state. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among a specified set of possible measures, which corresponds to enforcing low-frequency Fourier constraints through a convex program. The uniqueness and stability of this solution are examined under various conditions, specifically when the Fourier constraints become incomplete (Kc < infinity). To overcome the inherent nonidentifiability in such inverse problems, a statistical approach is employed to provide both upper and lower bounds for the total variation of the estimated measure relative to the true measure, thereby ensuring stability. The uniqueness of solutions in a specific norm is also demonstrated and further extended to obtain a stability estimate through a weighted total variation metric. The proposed method is comparable to a maximum likelihood approach and yields a stable solution that converges asymptotically at a rate of O(√(log(n)/n}) in a specific weighted total variation metric and at a rate of O(1/√(log(n)/n}) in a metric corresponding to the L1 norm. The statistical approach is based on a novel technique for bounding the complexity of convex optimization problems through the analysis of Gaussian complexities. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions to open problems related to transportation-based models, specifically the standard model for flow networks and the logit model. Due to the nature of these models, their solutions exhibit discontinuities, making them challenging to optimize. Focusing on a specific subclass of differentiable potentials, we define a generalized gradient flow and establish its connection with a time-evolution version of the model. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate the existence of solutions and derive key properties, including monotonicity and energy dissipation. Interestingly, the time-evolution solution exhibits the same characteristics as the gradient flow, even in the absence of assumptions typically required for such flows. To optimize the model, we utilize a time-average approach and show that the optimal solution can be obtained by minimizing a criterion function, leading to a new interpretation of the model in relation to generalized monotone operators. Ultimately, these results facilitate the development of an efficient algorithm for solving the optimization problem, and through numerical experiments, we verify the efficiency of this method in comparison with standard methods. In particular, we observe that the time-average approach enables the convergence of the solutions toward the optimal solution when the model parameters satisfy specific boundedness conditions. In contrast, the solutions may converge erratically toward the optimal solution when the model parameters are unbounded. To address this issue, we propose a regularization technique that replaces the unbounded logit model with a bounded logit model, yielding a new solution that approaches the optimal solution in the limit as the regularization parameter vanishes. Notably, the proposed algorithm is capable of approximating the new solution when the regularization parameter is sufficiently small. production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing

checker and is shown to work with challenging examples like self-energy and 
vertex integrals and two-loop box integrals. Additionally, it can be extended to 
three-loop electroweak and mixed electroweak-QCD corrections, making it a 
general strategy for solving complex mathematical equations in particle 
physics. Pair production of charged Higgs bosons is an example of its 
practical applications, leading to more precise predictions than previously 
available. This technique can be freely accessed on the GHENT site.

The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. By integrating state-of-the-art techniques for surface code error correction, such as magic state preparation and high-throughput syndrome extraction, we've successfully demonstrated a functioning fault-tolerant QAOA circuit on a superconducting quantum processor. Specifically, our proof-of-concept implementation emulated a QAOA circuit with a single QAOA layer to solve the maximum independent set problem on a particular graph, achieving an approximation ratio of 81 percent. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either lack a clear direction for gradient descent or induce artificial obstacles along the way. We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive, dense feature set, which not only facilitates convergence but also enhances the model's ability to handle OoD scenarios. This method, known as Dense Initialization for Generalization (DIG), is uncomplicated and can be applied seamlessly to existing models, offering improved performance and generalized capability. Furthermore, DIG has the benefit of accelerating the optimization process and reducing the likelihood of overfitting, as evidenced by our experimental findings. Notably, DIG exhibits exceptional performance in robust deep learning applications, such as model distillation and data-free learning, as demonstrated by our experimental results. Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including 1% Tulip Red fluorescence dye. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in forming intricate structures with high precision and rapid convergence. Measurements have shown that our system can achieve high levels of image clarity, with associated root-mean-square wavefront errors in the order of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.3 waves for 120, 220, and 450 grit diffusers, respectively. Furthermore, we've observed a rapid decrease in our algorithm's iteration times with increasing grit sizes from 45 to 120, 220, 450. Specifically, our observed iteration times were in the range of 50 ms to seconds for different scenarios. To evaluate our system's potential in biomedical applications, we've demonstrated the ability to focus a 633 nm wavelength laser beam through 5 mm of chicken tissue containing 1% Tulip Red fluorescence dye with a calculated transmission efficiency of 1.81%, corresponding to a 633 nm wavelength laser beam. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring a high-energy particle detector function rely heavily on the use of a substrate during sensor fabrication. Although various CMOS sensor technologies exist, sensors built on high-resistivity Czochralski (CRC) substrates exhibit exceptional performance due to enhanced radiation resistance and higher signal quality. In this study, researchers investigated the properties of CMOS sensors on resistive CRC substrates with a focus on high-energy particle detection efficiency. In-depth analysis revealed that sensors utilizing an anode layer at the sensor's entrance achieve a considerable enhancement in hit-detection rate and overall system efficiency, amounting to a 1.5 times increase, when compared to standard epitaxial materials. Furthermore, computational models validate that increased signal quality and signal persistence in CRC materials substantially contribute to enhanced detection efficiency. In conclusion, sensors on high-resistivity CRC substrates demonstrate improved performance and greater flexibility for further technological advancements. These advantages make this technology particularly suitable for future monolithic sensor systems. Such systems will serve as a fundamental component in scientific and medical applications, including particle physics, medicine, and industry. Specifically, they will soon underlie the CMS tracker system upgrade. In addition to its continued use in various projects such as SHAW, we are currently preparing for mass production of such sensors in large-scale initiatives including the CMS tracker upgrade and the BGO DIRC system for Oz project. In this context, researchers are exploring ways to fine-tune industrial sensor production to minimize costs while maximizing performance and flexibility of the final product. A key aspect in achieving this is to standardize sensor properties through control of relevant parameters in the sensor fabrication process. A thorough investigation of relevant technological parameters and their impact on final sensor performance has been conducted, and the findings have been presented in detail in the accompanying report. Based on the results, multiple paths for optimizing sensor performance were identified, and their potential to enhance radiation resistance, signal quality, and electrical properties of the sensors has been confirmed. In particular, introducing a metal layer beneath the anode in the sensor's entrance has been shown to significantly improve detection efficiency while meeting strict requirements for electrical properties. Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds. In a more recent experiment, we integrated FAST with the Gemini Planet Imaging Zoo, a computer simulator that models the atmosphere and telescope's effects, demonstrating its ability to eliminate the combined distortions of both the atmosphere and telescope with an evaluation accuracy of around 70 ns. This breakthrough demonstrates that FAST can effectively eliminate the distortions of ground-based telescopes equipped with advanced adaptive optics systems such as the Gemini Observatory's Gemini Planet Imaging Zoo, with an evaluation accuracy of around 70 ns. This significant advancement brings us one step closer to successfully eliminating the distortions of large ground-based telescopes and will significantly increase our ability to spot and study distant planets. With the potential to process images at an incredible speed of around 10,000 photons per second, FAST is now more than capable of effectively eliminating the distortions of future large ground-based telescopes. This remarkable speed will enable the detection and study of numerous celestial objects never before seen, including the planets and stars of our Milky Way galaxy. Next, we will integrate FAST with the upcoming massive 39-meter to 49-meter telescopes in the Extremely Large Telescope program, a project that will further expand our ability to spot and study the diverse range of celestial objects in our universe. Finally, we would like to emphasize the significant potential of FAST to not only eliminate the distortions of telescopes but also to discover new features and applications in the field of astronomy. With its incredible ability to process images at an incredible speed, FAST will play a vital role in discovering new technologies and techniques that will shape the future of astronomical discoveries. In the near future, we and our collaborators plan to test the capabilities of FAST in the actual environment of the actual telescopes

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives. Generally, we found that DUNE's capabilities will enable discoveries in which the difference between the mass of the sterile neutrino and its associated decay width is less than 10 MeV. Specifically, for a 70 kiloton Near Detector equipped with a 3-year run of DUNE, we anticipate the following limitations: a 10 GeV mass scale for electron and muon neutrinos, a higher mass scale for tau neutrinos due to its longer decay length. These projections assume neutrinos produced in neutrino-induced background and that the detector's far mode is not influential in determining these limits. Consequently, we suggest running DUNE with a 20 neutron equivalent flux from a 17.5 km long neutrino beam to further decrease background, resulting in a more stringent limit. Ultimately, this could result in a 10 GeV mass scale for tau neutrinos. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with a small number of studies, several new estimators have been developed.  We introduce four novel estimators that control for both within and across study correlations, also investigating two existing estimators with similar properties.  Through comprehensive simulation studies we assessed the performance of these estimators in scenarios of varying within and across study correlations, also examining their use in published meta-analyses.  Results indicated that three of the new estimators and two of the established estimators maintained accurate p-value estimates in cases of a small number of studies.  However, both established estimators struggled to accurately account for within study correlations.  When conducting meta-regressions, two of the new estimators were found to provide consistent bias variance estimates, compared to the existing estimators.  In order to facilitate easy implementation of these new approaches, corresponding R code is available within the meta2r package.  As such packages as meta, metafor and robust  do not currently support robust cluster robust variance estimators, it is necessary to utilize the meta2r package for these tasks.  In order to facilitate the comparison of performance between estimators, a publicly available repository includes reproducible code for creating figures and results tables.
