Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. Furthermore, this study serves as a systematic introduction to the application of topological categories in modal logic. In particular, it covers key concepts in modal logic such as modal translation, correspondence theory, and modal definability, as well as the fundamental properties of modal logic that stem from the semantics in preliminaries. By doing so, this work provides a unified presentation of the existing methods in the field. Additionally, this study limits its focus to a specific subset of modal logic known as normal modal logic and excludes other forms of modal logic. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI enables seamless access to a variety of COPASI functions, including model editing, simulation sets, and statistical analysis, among others. Furthermore, users can upload their own models and share them on a public dashboard, while also being able to run tasks remotely and receive notifications when results are available. The implementation of ShinyCOPASI has greatly expanded user capabilities and convenience. For example, users can now run time-course simulations in parallel using multiple cores, and view the results immediately. The development of ShinyCOPASI has significantly reduced technical barriers, making it easy for users to perform complex tasks and obtain a wealth of information with just a few clicks. As a result, users can perform an average of 5 tasks per day, a rate that is 16 times higher than before the platform's introduction. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its reformulation as a nonlinear equation problem, we present Newton's method as a policy iteration alternative. Although it faces similar local issues, a specially designed acceleration technique allows it to take larger-than- $\sqrt{\mathcal{S}}$ steps in its iterations, where $\mathcal{S}$ represents the number of states. Furthermore, when combined with a suitable approximation of the gradient of its objective function, this method achieves a complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\log(1/\epsilon)/\beta)$ for achieving desired accuracy $\epsilon$ with contraction rate $\beta$. However, for many critical applications such as reinforcement learning in game theory, gradient information may be unavailable. In this case, we introduce a novel, data-independent technique based on the idea of harmonic moments that allows us to estimate the gradient when action-value function approximations are available. This method reduces the cost of policy evaluation to $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{A}|^2 \log^3(\mathcal{S})/\beta^2)$, where $\mathcal{A}$ represents the number of actions. This expense enables the application of Newton's method in large-scale Markov decision processes. A comparable approach also is developed for linearly conjugate duality problems. In our experiments, this method surpasses several established algorithms in its performance. Additionally, its convergence in its iterations has been proven to be globally quadratic when its preconditioner is an oracle for computing the next policy. Finally, theoretical bounds show that the cost of computing this preconditioner can be reduced by first performing policy iteration on a limited state space. In our experiments, this strategy offers significant improvements in both efficiency and effectiveness. In light of its promising performance, we nickname this method the Harmonic Method. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based model as a more robust alternative to mean-based models, which are prone to being disrupted by outliers. This method offers the ability to synthesize durations at arbitrary timesteps, resulting in more natural transitions between phones. Experiments using the Freespeech corpus demonstrate that this approach outperforms exponential and normal models, with median-based models exhibiting fewer abrupt phrase endings and a more gradual decline in ending pauses over time. Additionally, this method can be used to generate artificial data, leading to improved model performance when used in place of real data in limited-corpus training. In particular, this artificial data enabled a model based on n-grams to outperform a deep-basis model in terms of MOS, with median-based models excelling over exponential and normal models in all scenarios. Both natural and artificial data generated by this method were found to be more comparable to human pause patterns than those produced by traditional models. Overall, this new duration modelling technique exhibits numerous advantages, with potential applications including more realistic speech pauses, tailoring models to specific datasets, and generating artificial data, as evidenced by further analyses using the Wizard of Oz dataset. This new approach led to improved model performance, as measured by MOS, when used for speech synthesis. Specifically, models trained using this method outperformed those trained using the original Freespeech dataset in terms of naturalness, with gains of 0.25 and 0.14 in median-based and uniform models, respectively. Furthermore, this technique displayed versatility in models based on n-grams and deep bases, indicating broad applicability across different model architectures. Additional analyses using the Wizard of Oz dataset showed that this method produced more naturally occurring pause patterns, thereby demonstrating a closer alignment between the generated pause times and those observed in human speech. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning, deep learning, and gamification to enhance both precision and efficiency. The new diagnostic tool was created by building upon existing IML, deep learning specifically deep neural networks, and gamified decision support systems. In particular, the project introduced a novel IML approach for data augmentation, a new deep neural network model for image diagnosis, and a comprehensive evaluation of the system's reliability. The Skincare project's results showed significant improvements in accuracy and speed, both in training and testing stages. The base case showed a 26% faster diagnosis time, with the IML approach taking an additional 30% to 50% time. The general practitioners' accuracy improved from 58.9% to 66.4%, with the deep learning model reaching 82.3% accuracy. The gamified approach increased precision by 23% to 38%, and the IML-gamified method further boosted it to 42% to 54% or 46.2% overall. Consequently, the Skincare system presented a more efficient and effective diagnostic tool for malignant skin lesions. The project's findings also suggested potential future applications in other medical image categorization areas. The new diagnostic tool has the potential to support both dermatologists and non-expert practitioners in their daily work, thereby reducing diagnosis times and improving overall precision. in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user

circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient.

we utilize an epidemiological model coupled with real data from WhatsApp in Brazil, 
India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay the spread of information but are ultimately insufficient to 
halt the dissemination of highly viral misinformation campaigns within public groups. 
Consequently, we recommend combining these technical measures with the removal of 
accounts that host such groups and contribute to the rapid spread of misinformation.

election periods, appears to be an effective strategy to contain the impact of 
unverified information on social media platforms like WhatsApp. Our investigation 
provides valuable insights for WhatsApp moderators, researchers, and users alike, 
highlighting various techniques to combat the misuses of WhatsApp during rapid 
information dissemination. Conversely, our study also emphasizes the importance of 
preserving anonymity and encryption to prevent unwarranted access to user 
communications. Furthermore, we stress the necessity of balancing both these 
considerations, ultimately aiming for an equilibrium that prioritizes the 
preservation of anonymity and encryption while effectively addressing the 
misinformation issues on WhatsApp. In achieving this goal, we propose an 
experimentation pipeline consisting of qualitative ethnographic investigations 
alongside quantitative data analysis from WhatsApp, which can provide valuable 
insights for platform moderators, researchers, and users, ultimately leading to 
the development of more effective countermeasures against the rapid spread of

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure. Key words: Branching process, frequency spectrum, central limit theorems, Extended Haplotype Homozygosity, infinite alleles model. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 60J80, 62E17. ```

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Notably, we found that our AReLU-based system outperformed existing state-of-the-art spoof detection methods on this dataset. Our experimental results indicate that the incorporation of AReLU results in a 4% enhancement in overall performance. We also obtained a 2% improvement in F-score when using this technique to train our feature extraction model, which is another significant advantage. We believe that introducing AReLU as a adaptable activation layer has the potential to be a versatile and effective tool in the development of additional AEC methods. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to understand how its principles can explain fundamental observations such as inflation.  Despite its potential, constructing in inflationary models in supergravity is a significant challenge due to several issues, including the memory of the original quantum fluctuations from the early universe known as brane inflationary fluctuations.  A recent study in arXiv:2206.17812 highlights these challenges and discusses potential solutions in a new class of supergravity models called SUGRAfolds.  These SUGRAfolds are characterized by their simplicity and ability to be easily integrated into a more comprehensive theory, making them an attractive option for addressing the challenges mentioned above.  A primary goal of this work is to make SUGRAfolds accessible to a broader audience, including cosmologists, through a simplified overview of its components, instead of delving into the more complex mathematical intricacies involved in supergravity.  A related work in arXiv:2206.17817 examines the potential of SUGRAfolds in addressing cosmological concerns, focusing on the potential risks of instability in the inflationary model.  A preliminary study in arXiv:2111.02429 initially explored the concept of SUGRAfolds, in which new types of supergravity models were introduced as alternatives to the more conventional Kaluza-Klein inflationary models.  These SUGRAfolds are characterized by their ability to transfer the brane inflationary fluctuations to the bulk scalar field, similar to the approach in the old inflationary theory.  Initial findings suggested that the SUGRAfolds can be designed to meet the Necessity Conditions of the inflationary model, including the requirement that the bulk scalar field should be able to move across the extra dimension without being impeded by any potential barrier.  However, the Stability Condition of the inflationary model, which states that the stability of the vacuum should be maintained, is not satisfied in the SUGRAfold models based on the RS1 extra dimension.  Consequently, the SUGRAfold inflationary model needs to be modified to ensure that it meets the requirements of a more comprehensive theory, such as string theory. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we outline potential applications of terahertz SNOM in evaluating Josephson junction critical currents and detecting local ion impurities in aluminum resonators. Ultimately, our research aims to facilitate the development of better materials for superconducting quantum computing. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in the simulated market, the financial gains of both the CTA and SRT increased substantially when both traders engaged in strategic trading activities. This symbiotic relationship was found to be the direct result of the dynamic interaction between the fundamental and market-making aspects of both traders' activities. It was also observed that the profits of both traders peaked when both engaged in frequent trading. In a real-world commodity trading setting, this could be interpreted as a potential risk-reward scenario where CTAs and SRTs may both benefit from collaborating and engaging in more active trading. The research offers a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between these traders and their potential for collaborative profitability. Further studies are recommended to investigate (i) how the spatial distribution of traders affects market dynamics and (ii) whether the CTA-SRT relationship remains stable in the presence of varying market conditions and trading strategies. In a related area of inquiry, it is suggested that future research could explore the benefits of collaborative trading between CTAs and other types of traders. This could be accomplished by incorporating an electronic broker into the market who matches trades and sends signals to both the CTA and SRT. As an added layer of complexity, the study proposes that the actions of all traders could be governed by a set of reward structures that encourage them to make decisions in the best interest of the market as a whole. This reward structure could be optimized using reinforcement learning techniques in a second phase of research. Ultimately, the goal of this research is to contribute to our understanding of the interaction between CTAs and SRTs and the development of strategies for improving market stability and promoting profitable trading outcomes for all participants. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom. The precise manipulation of magnons could potentially lead to significant increases in storage capacity and performance in magnetic systems. Conversely, the magnetocrystalline anisotropy present in the recording of certain properties and other magnon systems may require alternative methods for controlling coherent magnons. The research in this paper focuses on a new method for controlling coherent magnons in ferromagnetic recording materials by leveraging the magnetostatic field generated by a superconducting gate. The experiment involved placing a superconducting gate on top of a 2-disk recording system comprised of Pt and CrO2 layers, both of which exhibit strong magnetostatic field resistance, in a specific setup. The recording system was initially set in a stable 180-degree magnetic arrangement before being exposed to a controlled external magnetic field that caused a frequency shift in the central record. A subsequent recording system reconfiguration resulted in a significant increase in the frequency difference between the two records, indicating a high level of magnon confinement. Theoretical modeling confirmed our experimental results, highlighting the potential for magnon confinement through the resistance of a magnetic field to external influences. The magnetostatic field generated by the superconducting gate can be adjusted to achieve a high level of magnon confinement similar to that found in the experiment, showing the promise of this new method for controlling coherent magnons in ferromagnetic materials. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Importantly, this study highlights the value of incorporating diverse news sources from across the country to understand the complex and nuanced interplay between local contexts and national pandemic trajectories. Furthermore, our findings emphasize the significance of considering both broadcast and print news, as well as online articles, in order to effectively reach all segments of the population disadvantaged by the decline in local news coverage. Finally, our research is crucial in informing efforts to combat misinformation and enhance public health communications during the pandemic and beyond. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. To achieve this, we found that the ESBN's latent layer was able to distinguish between the size of the items in the binary vector and their indices, effectively compressing complex data into easier-to-learn patterns. Additionally, our AI was able to generalize its learning across various item selection tasks by testing it with the 'is-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to determine the exact number 'N' - we observed that the ESBN's performance benefited greatly when its module responsible for handling the input data was modified to a more efficient structure. To validate the reliability of our results, we conducted extensive tests where we repeatedly trained and tested our AI under different conditions, and consistently observed the same patterns of behavior. To the best of our knowledge, our study presents the first simulation of the 'give-N' task using reinforcement learning, and our findings present valuable insights into the study of intelligence. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of our results, our source code, as well as videos illustrating our study, are publicly available for verification and reproduction at https://github.com/kr1p5/cognitive-milestones. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed Bloom filters. Comprehensive tests were conducted to evaluate the developed filters' accuracy and speed. A detailed comparison with existing solutions was also performed, demonstrating the advantages of the presented filters. A different approach was applied to construct a variant of the xor filter, resulting in the hybrid xor, a more efficient solution with less memory requirements. A step-by-step guide to implementing the hybrid xor was created and made available for public use. A different variation of the hybrid xor was also designed, leading to the triple xor. A different reconstruction strategy was used to construct this variant, resulting in less storage needs and comparable efficiency to existing solutions. A detailed analysis was conducted on the performance of the triple xor, revealing superior efficiency and speeds. A different compact variant of the triple xor was also designed (triple+), offering more effective efficiency and speeds along with less storage needs. A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those describing the time series of prices relative to future prices. This study modifies the basic supply and demand model to account for the time variation of prices relative to future prices, influenced by market forces such as the speed and direction of trading. By assuming that prices adjust slowly to changes in market dynamics, the model exhibits a fundamental characteristic of stability, despite the presence of nonlinearities. Furthermore, the model displays two distinct stable equilibrium points, representing superior and inferior limits on future prices. According to the model, the rate of price change is positively correlated with the difference between the current price and the superior limit, and negatively correlated with the difference between the current price and the inferior limit, both correlations being amplified by the convex relationship between prices and trade volume. This theoretical framework can be applied to financial markets using alternative price equations that are consistent with observed market phenomena, such as the relationship between prices and trade speed, the relationship between prices and volatility, and the relationship between prices and market capitalization. Specifically, the study uses empirical analysis of crude oil futures prices, confirming that trade volume does indeed influence price movement, particularly in relation to the market's upper price limit. This is demonstrated by a significant positive correlation between the difference between the current price and the superior limit and the rate of price change, and a significant negative correlation between the difference between the current price and the inferior limit and the rate of price change. In contrast, the relationship between prices and trade speed, the relationship between prices and volatility, and the relationship between prices and market capitalization do not exhibit the expected significance. Overall, the study reveals that market price movements can be influenced by the number of shares traded per unit time in relation to market capacity, specific trade behaviors, price movements in response to volatility, and market capitalization and liquidity levels. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. Moreover, it only incurs a minor performance decrease, compared to the baseline FL system. Notably, FLVoogd's ability to prevent data breaches and maintain user anonymity is crucial in contemporary machine learning applications where data ownership often resides with data providers. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/flashhll/FLVoogd. In terms of future work, we intend to expand FLVoogd's support to additional ML tasks and incorporate other security mechanisms such as privacy-protection techniques. Additionally, we aim to investigate FLVoogd's applicability in settings where data ownership is unclear. In the event that our study reveals any conflicts of interest, we disclose them in the paper as follows. Our research was partially funded through grants from the NSF N3C project and the Harvard Data Science Initiative. Harper Langston is a researcher at Harvest.ai, where he develops and publishes open-source software including FLVoogd. Our other contributors are listed in the author information section. Finally, our ethics statement is presented in Appendix D. Federation of learning systems has emerged as a promising solution to address privacy concerns while training AI models using distributed data. Nonetheless, the lack of robust security measures in FL exposes the system to malicious clients' attacks, which contaminate the learning process. To address this issue, we have developed FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that prevents Byzantine attacks while maintaining user privacy. Our approach is based on clustering client updates using data majority detection and distance-controlling testing, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets reveals FLVoogd's ability to block malicious submissions and preclude data exposure from the server at a minor performance cost. The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere atop a liquid water ocean would produce CO2 and N2, with the presence of photochemically produced CO and CH4, and reduced NH3 due to dissolution in the ocean. These atmospheric compositions produce distinctive features in the optical phase curves and transmission spectra of exoplanets, with the distinction being most pronounced for planets with masses of 2-3 Earth masses. Notably, different solubility coefficients for small atmospheres produce a distinctive feature in the near-infrared of the small atmosphere spectrum. Estimating the solubility coefficients for atmospheric gases in liquid water and identifying suitable biochemical markers for atmospheric gas absorption are essential for resolving the atmosphere mass mystery. Our study offers a promising strategy for resolving this long-standing enigma and assessing the habitability potential of sub-Neptune exoplanets. Leveraging the distinct properties of small vs. massive atmospheres could be crucial for solving the atmosphere mass puzzle and determining the habitability potential of temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets in future missions. Additionally, we provide essential guidelines for ocean carbon and nitrogen cycling in liquid water atmospheres to facilitate comparisons with future observational data and candidate planet characteristics. These guidelines are particularly important for evaluating the habitability potential of exoplanets like K2-18b, for which future James Webb Space Telescope observations will be pivotal in resolving the atmosphere mass mystery and determining its habitability potential.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a vital role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. In direct bonding configurations, the energy levels at the interface equilibrate, resulting in similar energy levels on both sides. However, in indirect bonding configurations, the energy levels shift and become uneven. Specifically, the energy level of the EuS valence band maximum aligns with the InAs valence band maximum in all considered configurations. Introducing a weak interface bonding interaction results in a significant spillover effect, where the energy levels reshift, and the interface charge transfer increases. Notably, the energy bands of InAs remain relatively stable. In another variation, introducing a weak interface dipole interaction leads to the emergence of midgap states, which potentially act as acceptor states. The calculations also demonstrate that the electronic properties of InAs are insensitive to the choice of interface configuration. However, these properties are significantly affected by the bonding configuration. The study's findings could serve as a basis for guiding experiments and identifying potential magnetic InAs materials. Furthermore, the model's methodology, which combines machine-learned data and DFT, can be applied to the study of various interfaces to predict electronic properties. For the purposes of this study, the model is made publicly available on our website. Additionally, the data necessary to reproduce the results can be accessed through the provided link. Finally, possible applications of the interface in spintronics, magnetic memory, and quantum computing are discussed. The potential for further research in this domain is also explored. A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Additionally, we offer an interpretation of Borel Wadge classes as $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I semidecidable through a series of reductions. These achievements are contingent on a fundamental assumption about Borel Wadge classes being $\Pi^1_1$-I decidable. It has been proven that this assumption is both necessary and sufficient for the Borel Wadge determinacy theorem within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Furthermore, comparable results have been developed for sets of natural numbers, including the introduction of complete classification systems for subsets of $2^{\omega}$ and demonstrations of Borel Wadge determinacy within specific arithmetic systems. These achievements are contingent on certain assumptions about projective set theory and unbounded arithmetic, including $\text{ATR}_0+\forall\exists\Delta^1_1$. Additionally, we offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem and a comparison with Montalbán's true stage machinery for projects, as well as generalizations and applications of these results. These achievements provide the foundation for an extensive theory of Borel Wadge classes within systems of second-order arithmetic, including $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I, through a combination of complete classification systems, Borel Wadge determinacy theorems, and natural interpretations of Borel Wadge classes as semidecisible within these arithmetic systems. To bridge this gap, we introduce ClickTrain, a framework that facilitates both model optimization and deployment. Based on a trainable feature extractor, ClickTrain employs a novel block-wise clicking approach to the aggregator network. This approach enables the development of optimized models with reduced computational complexity while retaining accuracy. Subsequently, the trainable feature extractor is utilized as a domain-specific knowledge container to enable efficient model deployment on edge devices. Notably, ClickTrain demonstrates an ability to accurately reconstruct input images using the retained knowledge, demonstrating its feasibility. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a probabilistic method called Bayes's theorem, which enables the rapid classification of signals in real-time. Using the Bayes's theorem approach, we have achieved 90% accuracy in distinguishing binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole mergers, using only the inspiral gravitational wave signal, in simulations mimicking future detector capabilities. Furthermore, we have developed a tool to facilitate the rapid classification of events in real-time, incorporating Bayes's theorem. This tool is designed for use in online analyses of future gravitational wave data and has been made publicly available. With future detectors set to detect numerous gravitational wave events, incorporating Bayes's theorem will facilitate critical contributions to neutron star research, particularly through the segmentation of gravitational waves into distinct phases. Applying this approach will grant scientists the ability to examine the properties of neutron star dense matter in greater detail. Moreover, this method will also enable the separation of binary neutron star events and neutron star-black hole mergers, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of these events, such as their magnetic field configuration, based on their gravitational wave signatures. Ultimately, the integration of Bayes's theorem will provide a more thorough ground for incorporating gravitational waves into electromagnetic analyses, thereby providing a more accurate and in-depth understanding of neutron star behavior. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to learn policies for CMDPs in a model-free setting: (1) identifying states and actions that comply with specific constraints, and (2) efficiently exploring the policy search space to identify a viable solution. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the concept of a constraint map, which facilitates the discovery of valid state-action pairs. We then propose the iterative Q-learning with constraint propagation (IQ-PCP) algorithm to tackle these issues. IQ-PCP is a two-part approach that utilizes both an off-policy algorithm and a forward simulation technique to efficiently discover a feasible policy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IQ-PCP through simulation tests based on the new product development problem. Our findings show that IQ-PCP successfully discovers a viable policy in both clean and noisy environments, and that its computation time is more efficient than alternative approaches. We also demonstrate the superiority of IQ-PCP in a real-world new product development case study. Our analysis reveals that IQ-PCP's performance is sensitive to various parameters, such as the reward structure and initial state action assignments. As such, future research could focus on investigating these sensitivities and developing techniques to handle multiple constraints governing sequential decision-making problems. Ultimately, we aim to establish a comprehensive understanding of the feasibility of learning constraints in a model-free setting. Our findings contribute to this goal, and provide a framework for solving a broad class of problems governed by constraints in a sequential decision-making context. Our work also lays the groundwork for future research into the learning constraints problem, and explores its relevance to a range of applications in operations management, such as new product development and supply chain contract design. As such, our study provides a valuable contribution to the field of operations management, and sheds light on the capabilities and limitations of learning constraints in a model-free setting. A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 3D hyper-Kahler symplectic manifold: an accumulation point of BPS state degeneracy growth rates would imply a refutation of a previously proposed conjecture by Jeffrey-Kang. A distinct case is the quantum orbifold chart $X_{3}\rightarrow X$, where the growth rates of BPS states conform to Polyak-Danilov's prediction, thereby validating their conjecture. A simplified representation is also introduced for expressing the growth rates of BPS states in superconformal quantum mechanics based on a general hyper-Kahler symplectic resolution. Additionally, a distinct simplification is introduced for resolving the symmetric product of a complex curve with genus one. Finally, a novel table is presented that documents the growth rates of BPS states for a selection of symplectic resolutions. Specifically, the tables for resolving local rational curves, nilpotent Hodge bundles, and the space of complex lines in a hyper-Kahler symplectic manifold all conform to Polyak-Danilov's prediction for the growth rates of BPS states. Conversely, the growth rates of BPS states in the Hilbert scheme of points, the double cover over the minimal resolution of an A_2 singularity, and the second symmetric product of a complex curve with genus one all fail to conform to this prediction. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to cause a secondary outbreak of infections, resulting in two distinct periods of variability. Specifically, the large fluctuations in the early stages of an epidemic within local clusters pose significant challenges to forecasting its spread. Crucially, our analysis suggests that bridging elements within the network have a substantial impact on predictability, with increased distances between these elements to distant regions of the network significantly hindering forecast accuracy. Furthermore, this predictability challenge is likely to persist even after widespread vaccination, as the residual network architecture following such an event continues to exhibit community structures. Hence, targeting key contacts involved in information exchange within social groups, i.e., seed contacts, is crucial for enhancing the efficacy of contact tracing efforts. Additionally, our research provides a mathematical relationship for estimating the minimum number of Seed contacts required to achieve a predictable outcome. Finally, despite the underlying network's complexity, we found that the basic Reproductive Number $R_{0}$ remains a reliable indicator of epidemic risk, and as such can be used effectively to guide public health strategies in heterogeneous contact networks. Moreover, our analysis shows that the emergence of an epidemic in such networks can be effectively suppressed through targeted intervention measures, and as an added bonus, the associated loss of business activity is significantly reduced when compared to a uniform contact tracing approach. In particular, our research highlights that the proximity of Seed contacts to each other, rather than their distance from other groups within the network, is the key factor that distinguishes successful from unsuccessful tracing events. Our comprehensive study provides valuable insights both from both epidemiological and network science perspectives that can contribute to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. In the long term, the concepts and techniques developed here can also be applied to other infectious disease outbreaks and generalized to various types of heterogeneous contact networks. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in reducing the gap between the approximated posterior and optimal policy distribution. Furthermore, our approach optimizes exploration within actor-critic learning by guiding the exploration towards high-dimensional areas in the policy search space. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted extensive simulations using two diverse environments - a simple cart-pole system and the hard-exploration environment of Vizdoom - and observed significantly enhanced performance in both scenarios. Specifically, our results revealed a 25% enhancement in the learning speed of the Hamiltonian Policy compared to the standard actor-critic model. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are modified, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either operating in isolation or within a swarm of robots. By creating a 2D map of the environment, the robot generates a safe and secure navigation route. Leveraging the strengths of the sonar sensor, the algorithm achieves close-range measurements, determining obstacles' widths and depths, as well as their relative motion. These enhancements enable the implementation of a more advanced trajectory planner that ensures the robot maintains a safe distance from detected obstacles. In simulated tests, the proposed method demonstrated successful operation in a variety of scenarios, including both IR- and sonar-only conditions. Notably, the approach displayed improved performance in navigating tighter spaces and closely spaced obstacles. The simulated results support the method's potential for practical application in mobile robots, indicating a significant reduction in navigation time when compared to a more basic trajectory planner. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds historical significance, was studied in 2002-2007 through a series of observations using the Hubble Space Telescope. These observations revealed changes in Nereid's highly reflective white color as it orbited varying backgrounds. It was observed that the surface reflection strength increased by approximately 0.3 magnitude as it moved from the direction of the Sun to the direction of Neptune. Following that, the team detected a subtle, brown-hued dust cloud surrounding the planet. Additionally, the spectral variation could be partially attributed to volatiles such as water and methane, which are thought to condense and vaporize in response to Nereid passing through the pericenter of its highly eccentric orbit. Based on further analysis, the researchers concluded that the cloud and volatile effects are likely responsible for most, if not all, of the observed spectral changes. Utilizing photometric modeling, the team was also able to place constraints on the extent and opacity of the cloud, as well as the thermal emission produced by the satellite's warm interior. Notably, the study found the satellite's surface temperature to be approximately 40 K. Building on this research, the team made comparisons with other similar objects in the solar system, including Neptune's other satellites and the Kuiper Belt object, 2007 VM84. In the process, the study contributed to a broader understanding of the thermal evolution and internal dynamics of these small, icy satellites. Information about the satellite's size and composition was also determined in conjunction with this research, as well as with observations made using the Hubble Space Telescope in 2004, the Keck II telescope in 2005, and the Spitzer Infrared Space Telescope in 2006-2007. As a result, the team was able to determine that the satellite's diameter is approximately 340 kilometers. Furthermore, the team used these observations in conjunction with data from the study of Nereid's gravitational effect on the motion of other satellites in the system to determine the density of the satellite. Based on this information, the team was able to determine the satellite's composition, which consists primarily of water ice with smaller amounts of rocky material. Lastly, the study marked an important milestone in the ongoing exploration of the solar system by validating a long-standing prediction that the entrapment of satellites by parent planets is possible, as demonstrated through the example of Nereid and Neptune. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our method learns this parameter as part of the Bayesian learning process, by introducing a set of "caution" variables that adapt to the availability of data-dependent information. By incorporating these variables into the Markov decision process, a new Bayesian learning method is developed, which uses Monte Carlo simulations to estimate the optimal action. Theoretical and simulated evidence confirm the method's convergence and superior performance compared to alternative pessimism-based methods. The method is further evaluated through applications to two public health crises, influenza and HIV, resulting in improved treatment recommendations with our new method. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this phenomenon, we examine a simplest type of flat band superconductor, an s-wave superconductor consisting of two coupled bosonic Weyl nodes. Through a combination of analytical methods including Bethe ansatz and quasinormal mode expansion, we investigate how coupling between nodes affects key properties like critical temperature, superconducting gap, and critical magnetic field. We also explore how these characteristics are altered when electron interactions become more complex, assuming electrons follow the same path in both normal and superconducting states, as in the case of Fock clustering. Our studies have shown that increased electron interaction enhances critical temperatures, reduces superconducting gaps, and transforms the critical magnetic field behavior, as evidenced by phase diagram computations. Additionally, we outline potential experimental routes for verifying our theoretical findings, involving measurements of thermal conductivity, specific heat, NMR, and transport phenomena like the anomalous Hall effect and thermal Hall effect. Finally, we demonstrate that the superconductor under scrutiny exhibits some extraordinary properties, including the ability to efficiently transport triplets while unpaired electrons remain stationary, in addition to the ability to increase triplet pairing correlation through electron pairing, as seen in the case of heavy Fermon pairing, even in the presence of electron correlations as seen in the \kappa-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu(NCS)$_2$ material. Furthermore, we investigate how these characteristics are altered when an external electric field is applied, assuming that the field influences electron interaction in a nonlinear, nonuniform manner. Our findings have shown that the field can induce an electric charge gap in the electron system, as seen in the phase diagram computed using our proposed model for field-induced superconductivity. Additionally, we outline the ability to use transport phenomena, as seen in the case of the Anomalous Nernst and Anomalous Hall effects, to verify our theoretical findings. Lastly, as our theoretical model is applicable across a wide array of chalcogenide superconductors, our results have substantial practical significance for materials like Ba$_{1-x}$K$_{x}$Fe$_2$As$_2$ with $x\approx 0.3$, in addition to materials like (TMTSF)$_2$PF$_6$ and $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu(NCS)$_2$, by verifying the accuracy of our theoretical predictions across a wide array of experimental measurements. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. Clustering methods can analyze and group items based on their characteristics in ecological studies, but the application of such methods is limited in sociological research, despite its various uses in the field. This study proposes a novel clustering approach for binary data, aiming to improve the accuracy and efficiency of clustering results. The proposed method utilizes the statistical characteristics of binary data, allowing for the adjustment of model assumptions and the optimization of clustering results. This approach achieves higher clustering validity compared to traditional methods in simulated and real-world data sets, as evidenced by our findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in sociological research through two case studies. The first case involves determining the most suitable clustering method for binary data, while the second involves identifying species groups based on their presence in ecosystems. The proposed method outperformed existing methods in the first case and provided valuable insights into the taxonomic classification of species in the second case. The utility of our approach has been incorporated into the R package clustab. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, this unified structure is capable of producing competitive results for other image segmentation tasks, as demonstrated by experimental analysis. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants. We discuss the outcomes, identify potential areas for enhancement, and outline future research paths for further improvement. Additionally, the source code and pre-trained models utilized in this study are available on GitHub for public access at https://github.com/um-iu-ling/semeval-2019-offense-detection. We intend to maintain and update the repository regularly to ensure consistency with the latest developments in the field of Natural Language Processing. A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored, specifically how they can be expressed as the sum or difference of two identical values. We are looking to establish the most efficient way possible. A notable instance of this relationship is the observation that 26 can be expressed as the difference between 89 and 81. It's now our goal to determine if a natural number, N, can always be found such that (2N + 1)^2 is a palindrome but not a perfect square. If so, what is the smallest possible value of N? As an added challenge, is it always possible to find a natural number, N, such that (2N + 1)^2 is both a palindrome and a perfect square? If so, what is the smallest possible value of N? These questions have been answered for the case of fifth-power palindromes, so a similar investigation will be conducted for the case of seventh-powers, seeking the smallest values of N that satisfy the criteria. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical reconstructions of data collected from a test setup. Notably, the calculated quantum defects demonstrate the significant impact that incorporating the effects of polyenergetic X-rays and radiation has on image quality. A justifiable approximation of the non-convex optimization problem is also offered, and validated with various kinds of noise. Finally, the proposed method has been found to yield accurate and noise-reduced images in both theoretical and practical applications. A significant advantage of this model lies in its ability to achieve accurate attenuation coefficients with minimal artifacts, making it suitable for accurate phase retrieval in x-ray phase tomography. In addition, the proposed method provides a viable solution for total variation denoising, and has been found to produce reconstructions that align closely with actual values in both homogeneous and heterogeneous materials. A range of simulated and real data examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. For instance, accurate metal detection with reconstructed images featuring sharp metal boundaries is achieved, and the average relative error in attenuation coefficients for both plastic and metal materials has been found to be less than 0.05. Furthermore, the proposed method has been found to provide superior results compared to other existing methods in various kinds of noise environments. Finally, the proposed approach has been found to provide accurate and reliable reconstructions of data collected from actual 3D objects using X-ray Computed Tomography technology. In conclusion, the proposed model offers an efficient and accurate method for image reconstruction and chemical analysis in X-ray Computed Tomography technology. To further verify the proposed method, a range of real data examples have been provided, demonstrating its effectiveness and accuracy in various kinds of noise environments. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution. It is made freely available under the BSD-2 license at https://github.com/Graphine/BPL-HTR. This repository includes the BPL model implementation, the proposed dataset consisting of simulated ciphers, as well as the used HTR model and related resources. We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrices with more precise limits in ab initio calculations. Our scheme enables us to reach more realistic interaction strengths, akin to those found in experimentally derived two-nucleon interactions. We have demonstrated its efficacy with large-scale calculations of $^6$He using the no-core hypertree method based on the JISP16 potential. Our study shows that the ground-state wave function of $^6$He has about 10^4 configuration states with high energy excitations limited to 20 MeV. We computed the total binding energy of $^6$He to be -23.01 MeV, which is close to the experimental value of -20.18 MeV. Our calculated two-nucleon removal reactions for $^6$He yield results that agree with experiments: about an order of magnitude better for energies up to 44 MeV and essentially comparable to non-perturbative quark model calculations for energies up to 100 MeV. We observed that the calculated two-nucleon correlation functions of $^6$He exhibit expected agreements with non-relativistic ab initio models. Our proposed storage approach provides significant computational enhancements that facilitate further investigations of $^6$He using more sophisticated many-body methods based on the ab initio calculation of three-nucleon interaction matrices. Moreover, our scheme may also be applicable to larger nuclei than we have studied here. Our scheme can be adapted to computational methods other than the no-core hypertree method, such as the ab initio coupled-cluster method, to compute the ground-state wave function and its energy with arbitrary precision. We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics. Specifically, we explore the interplay between topological properties and electronic transport, examining the influence of interactions on a topological phase, and utilizing a topological toy model to study quantum phase transitions and correlated transport characteristics. This introduction aims to provide an understanding of the fundamental principles of topological physics, equipping students to investigate the interplay between interactions, topological properties, and electronic transport in one-dimensional systems. By delving into the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, students develop the skills to analyze various quantum systems, applying principles of quantum many-body physics to probe quantum phase transitions, analyze transport phenomena, and investigate the concept of topological order. Furthermore, we include an appendix with additional resources for further study. By taking an educational approach rooted in the principles of quantum electronics, we strive to inspire students to explore the connection between topological physics and quantum electronics, driving innovative advancements in the field. Ultimately, the goal is to foster student independence, encouraging them to apply what they've learned to new topics and models, and equipping them to analyze and understand the most recent literature on quantum electronics. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately represents the asymptotic behavior of string theory amplitudes as z $\to \infty$. As a result, the obtained gravity amplitudes exhibit a more straightforward relationship with their corresponding flat space counterparts, displaying logarithmic discontinuities that decrease in magnitude as z increases. Building upon this extension, model-independent boundary behavior in type IIB string theory is investigated through the use of a point-like gauge, revealing a direct link between string theory amplitude ratios and their AdS counterparts. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing a pool of small and catonic memory blocks.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as well as high memory locality through its block layout model, thereby enhancing the performance of SMMO applications.  Comprehensive testing of DynaSOAr across 16 benchmarks demonstrated its superiority, with results including up to 86x and 111x performance improvements in numerical and scientific computations, respectively, along with the potential to support 54% more threads in parallel.  Given its open-source and easy-to-use design, DynaSOAr is an ideal choice for developers seeking to harness the full potential of GPU power for a range of applications.  Future plans for DynaSOAr involve expanding its capabilities to support generalized object-oriented programming directly on GPUs.  Ultimately, the expected outcome of this research is a significant acceleration in the execution of SMMO applications, including real-world programs, on SIMD devices via the DynaSOAr framework.  In particular, we anticipate a performance improvement of at least an order of magnitude in comparison to the current fastest solution. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. Experimental results from a 180nm CMOS test chip verify the proposed design's performance. It features a compact layout size of 55.5kt squares, operates within a 0.72V to 1.2V voltage range, consumes extremely low power at 0.24uW, and provides temperature readings with an error of 2.4% and 2.2% over the range from -20C to 125C for N-bit and 8-bit frequency sampling, respectively. It also possesses a fast wake-up time of 10us and is suitable for use in temperature monitoring within processors. In addition, the proposed design offers significant reductions in area and power consumption when compared to a conventional digital temperature sensor. While the hybrid scheme used in this temperature sensor outperforms several alternative temperature sensing techniques, these modes do have some advantages, including energy efficiency, but come with the drawback of reduced precision. Therefore, a comprehensive design strategy that suitably balances precision, area, power consumption, and implementation complexity can be employed to select the most suitable temperature sensing approach for a particular application. In this particular instance, the high precision required in temperature sensing demanded by processors calls for the use of the hybrid scheme. To further minimize power consumption in temperature sensing, the hybrid scheme can also be combined with binary search, reducing the number of frequency samples needed and consequently minimizing power consumption. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of entangling two photons, both of which are based on modifying two-beam interferometry experiments to create correlated phase-sensitive states of polarized photons. These approaches are theoretically described and experimentally verified, offering a practical solution for generating polarization-entangled photons on demand. Additionally, we demonstrate that both methods can generate the desired entangled states under realistic experimental conditions, as proven through a series of tomographic measurements. This research has the potential to open up new avenues in the exploration and application of quantum entanglement. Furthermore, as an added benefit, one of the proposed methods presents a novel method for creating orthogonal entanglement, which serves as a starting point for developing more complex entangled states and is expected to contribute to the advancement of quantum information technologies. This research may also find an applicable analogy in traditional quantum mechanics for use in educational purposes. It is worth noting that the name "quantum scissors" is registered trademark of NIST.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the algorithm has no information about future points, but after that, it can respond to each new point based on its previous experiences. Despite this, the paper shows that any such algorithm must have a competitive ratio of at least Omega(sqrt(log n)/log n) for 1-dimensional space, and Omega(d/(d-1)) in d dimensions, which is just a constant factor worse than the optimal offline t-spanners. Next, it presents specific online algorithms for constructing and updating geometric t-spanners in d dimensions, with stretch ratios of at most 2^O(d) and competitive ratios of at most 2^O(d) + o(1) (depending on the specific algorithm). These results demonstrate that the difference between online and offline geometric t-spanners can be quite small, with a constant factor difference of at most twice in d dimensions. The paper also establishes lower bounds on the competitive ratio for constructing and updating geometric 2-spanners in d dimensions, showing that any such algorithm must have a competitive ratio of at least 0.7693... / (d-1). Finally, it considers the problem of constructing and updating point sets with small doubling property, and presents specific online algorithms for d = 1, 2, 3 dimensions, as well as a general result for any dimension. Additionally, it presents a new doubling property theorem, showing that any such set must contain at least 2^Omega(d) points. These results lead to new lower bounds on the competitive ratio for constructing and updating geometric t-spanners in d dimensions. The paper considers the case of OMW, a random ordering model that was previously shown to be the hardest ordering model for one-dimensional space, and shows that it is also the hardest for R^d by reducing it to the multi-dimensional version of the Fourier Tailing Lemma. Finally, it establishes new lower bounds on the competitive ratio for constructing and updating geometric 2-spanners in d dimensions under the random ordering MW.
