This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, this method can be done in under 5 seconds, making it significantly faster. Crucially, given the small number of parameters, the model can be easily retrained using only a few sample sentences from the target domain, thereby achieving accurate results in this context. By contrast, existing approaches often require extensive retraining on large-scale corpora, making them impractical for domain adaptation tasks. We showcase the effectiveness of this technique in a domain adaptation setting, illustrating its ease of use and adaptability. Additionally, due to its simplicity and efficiency, this method serves as a viable baseline for evaluating semi-supervised learning techniques. We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the observation of nematic and smectic liquid crystalline phases within the studied systems. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for surface slippage and stationary regimes by applying standard theories, with the latter exhibiting characteristics akin to Overhauser surface friction. Conversely, the stick-slip regime defies explanation via current theoretical models due to the non-uniform stress distribution within the rough surface. This study provides essential insights into the phenomena of surface slippage and friction modes in complex liquids. Additionally, we present a method to determine local surface roughness through stress analysis. This study lays the groundwork for further research into the nature of surface slippage, with the primary goal of developing a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and utilizing small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly. Moreover, DINO's strengths extend to image recognition, as our results show an 88.9% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly on the ImageNet ILSVRC-2019 challenge dataset. Furthermore, DINO's capabilities were successfully applied to other vision tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with an 8.9% relative mAP improvement on ImageNet-TFO. Comprehensive information about the DINO backbone can be found in our GitHub repository. Ultimately, the DINO self-supervised method represents a powerful tool for vision tasks, offering a strong foundation for further research and development. As such, the DINO backbone can be considered a new standard for self-supervised ViT models, one that outperforms existing self-supervised approaches while uniquely capturing semantic structure. Additionally, our research shows that convolutional networks can achieve comparable results to ViT models by incorporating self-supervised pre-training, highlighting the critical role of unlabelled data in modern deep learning systems. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that the unique capabilities of ViT models make them more effective than convolutional networks for self-supervised vision tasks. By combining the vision transformer with the self-supervised learning paradigm, we achieved a breakthrough in vision performance, achieving a 4.6% relative mAP improvement over convolutional networks on ImageNet-TFO. As such, our research represents an important step towards unlocking the full potential of vision transformers in self-supervised learning applications. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, making it difficult to achieve desired results. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a technique called SEGA, which provides guidance during the image generation process through multiple prompt adjustments. SEGA's key contribution involves inserting virtual temporal stages into the prompting schedule, allowing for the incorporation of additional guidance stages. We also develop a diffusion guidance module, which maintains the integrity of the prompting schedule, using previously generated images as temporary proxies to isolate the desired generative developments at each guidance stage. To further enhance SEGA's capabilities, we employ techniques like label persistence, virtual stage scheduling, and early stage termination. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To approximate this concept in practice, we employ ensemble averaging and Monte Carlo sampling as theoretical justifications for quantifying uncertainty. Based on these findings, we introduce the concept of uncertainty validation, a rigorous testing method that helps detect when a predictive model has exceeded its reliable limits. Additionally, we utilize uncertainty quantification to enhance the efficiency of embedding data recovery processes. We believe that our research on uncertainty in predictive models will inspire future steganographic methods that are more robust and reliable. Ultimately, we aim for the development of a reversible steganography framework that is both user-friendly and adaptable to various applications. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results indicate that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, associated with different types of magnetic flux elements, and influenced by the varying spatial resolutions of the telescopes used. Additionally, the findings show that the larger magnetic flux elements exhibit faster drift speeds, and the results are consistent with previous studies using different techniques, highlighting the importance of observational details in understanding the properties of magnetic bright points. This research provides a foundation for exploring the dynamics of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, and their potential link to the smaller-scale structures in the solar corona. Additionally, the work highlights the value of using a robust and efficient algorithm for detecting magnetic bright points, and suggests improvements for future adaptations to include corona-derived magnetic feature data. This research laid the groundwork for a future project, aimed at investigating how the characteristics of magnetic bright points change with altitude, utilizing the data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph. Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved in complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by introducing different parameters that mimic traffic congestion, specifically investigating the effects of reduced microtubules and swirling structures on material transportation. Our simulations effectively demonstrate both the optimal material transportation in healthy neurons and the occurrence of congestion in neurons with abnormalities, illustrating the significance of both geometry and microtubule structure in facilitating optimal neural transport processes. Extensive detailed analysis and visualization are presented to explore and understand the relationship between material and geometric/microtubule structures in neurons. To validate our model's ability to predict transport patterns in real neurons, we examine correlations between our numerical results and actual data on neural transport kinetics, finding substantial agreement. Moreover, our study presents novel insights into the relationship between neural geometry and transport patterns, suggesting future research directions, which could contribute to understanding neural degeneration and related disorders. Finally, our work successfully integrates optimal design principles into modeling neural transport processes, enabling the identification of optimal strategies for enhancing material transportation in complex neural structures. These principles could potentially be applied to develop new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. This parametrized space contains extreme points including $J_1 = D_{1/2,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{\infty} = D_{0,1}$, an analogue of the Levenstein distance, both of which are metrics. Additionally, our investigation reveals that the space of probability measures on a finite set equipped with this modified metric has a continuous structure. This condition implies that the support of the probability measure $\mu_A$, consisting of the elements from set $A$, is closed, which is equivalent to being compact. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique that uses a learned blur model to apply realistic blur to sharp images not included in the initial training dataset. The proposed method consists of two components: a motion-aware data augmentation framework and a retinex-based model that accurately replicates blur from video degradation models, enabling the transformation of clear images into blurry ones without relying on preprocessed data. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach can significantly enhance existing models without significantly increasing their run time or storage requirements. Notably, when combined with an existing model that incorporates attention and multi-scale features, our method achieves exceptional deblurring performance on real-world datasets, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods on various metrics. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that addresses these issues. Our proposed approach involves collecting various scientific datasets, developing a framework to determine each dataset's unique characteristics, and utilizing these traits to create tailored challenge problems that highlight each dataset's capabilities. By applying this process, we're able to create a diverse set of benchmarking problems that showcase each dataset's value and rank models according to how well they perform on each individual dataset. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it, even when restricted to basic operations over ordered structures. A significant turning point in understanding CPT's expressive power came with its recognition of non-equivalence to Monadic Second-Order Logic (MSO) through the use of well-ordering on graph vertices. Building on this realization, several CPT-definable decision problems on graph classes have been established, with the exception of a key choice function problem. Specifically, we investigate whether, for a given graph class, a choice function that selectively applies a given property (CFI-query) is CPT definable. Our research shows that CFI-query is CPT definable on ordered graph classes, particularly those with a well-ordering, by demonstrating an algorithmic approach. Conversely, we identify a hierarchy of finite graph classes (consisting of graphs with a loop and edges but no other complexities) in which a selective choice function (CFI) is not CPT definable, with even a more limited polynomial-time decidability (by means of a fixed polynomial time bound) for these graph classes failing. Despite these negative findings, CFI-query becomes CPT definable on various expansions of these basic graph classes, such as those that incorporate a limited form of arithmetic. Our research also identifies a distinction in CPT definability between choice functions and more comprehensive first-order properties on graph classes. Finally, working within a fixed time bound, we can construct instances of graphs where a selective choice function (CFI) doesn't follow a polynomial time decision, even when significantly restricted to time O(n^{\frac{3}{2}}) or specifically O(n^{\frac{5}{4}}) for deciding if a given vertex has the chosen property. This research represents an expansion on the initially reported separation, CPT vs PTIME, up to the O(n^{\frac{5}{4}}) time restriction. As a byproduct of our research, a novel method in constructing large structures, consistent with a given time bound, has been developed within a general framework. This construction is adaptable to various logarithmic complexity classes, including those covered by MSO. A novel approach to this problem uses data from the Planck satellite, which conducted a survey of the cosmic microwave background radiation.  This data offers a means of estimating the number of such particles, known as the relic density, rather than their interactions with matter directly. This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The method relies on initial Rabi oscillations, employing
a controlled amplitude-modulated drive to create the maximally entangled state.
The study also examines entanglement entropy as a function of time for both the
Jaynes-Cummings and anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction models, utilizing a von Neumann
entropy metric. Notably, the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model is observed to demonstrate
two distinct periods of reduced entropy, whereas the Jaynes-Cummings model only
exhibits one minimised entropy interval. The proposed approach offers a practical
method for generating maximally entangled states in anti-polariton systems. The study
also extends this technique to develop maximally entangled states in two-qubit systems,
using a combination of both Jaynes-Cummings and anti-Jaynes-Cummings interactions, in
what is referred to as a CHAMIT system. The research confirms that the minimum entropy
levels in the CHAMIT system can be precisely controlled using the Rabi oscillation
technique, resulting in the maximally entangled connection of two qubit states. The
study validates that the Rabi oscillation technique is a versatile method for producing
entangled states in a variety of quantum systems. The method proposed is highly efficient
and can be easily implemented using currently available techniques to produce maximally
entangled states in anti-polariton systems, as well as connected pairs of qubit states in
the CMIT system. The method is seen to be exceptionally effective in the CMIT system,
yielding entangled connection nearly twice as fast as previously reported approaches. 
The method is primarily discussed in the context of being easily implementable using
the Rabi oscillation technique, though it is acknowledged that its practical application

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates diagnostic processes and achieves precise measurements of heart rate variability (HRV), which is a critical indicator of cardiovascular health. Notably, the proposed method successfully demonstrated better results in both signal quality and IBI accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, according to comprehensive evaluations on publicly available datasets. Our results indicate that this deep learning approach is an effective solution for remote health monitoring and wearables, enhancing the diagnostic efficacy of deep learning technology. Additionally, the proposed method has potential applications in Wearable technology and Telemedicine services. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms existing solutions in both signal quality and IBI accuracy, and successfully demonstrates accurate HRV analysis during high-impact motion. Further studies could explore the use of Tiramisu autoencoders for other medical signal processing tasks. A Python implementation of the proposed method is available for research purposes on the GitHub repository https://github.com/shivanshs/ECG-Denoising. A detailed description of the model and evaluation process is provided in the associated paper titled 'ECG denoising using a Tiramisu autoencoder for remote health monitoring', published on BioRxiv https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2020/04/02/2020.03.04.981243. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture 37,219 individual views of 449 subjects performing a wide range of activities. Using these multi-view images, we demonstrate through qualitative and quantitative evaluations that HUMBI surpasses existing monocular and multi-view datasets in terms of reconstruction accuracy and reliability. The dataset is paired with a custom-built, high-performance, real-time mesh rendering engine known as HUMBI-RE, enabling efficient, high-definition human body representations suitable for use in advanced virtual try-on applications. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations, allowing it to adapt and fine-tune a universal neural model on a single monolingual dataset. We then demonstrate the robustness and versatility of our technique by effortlessly adapting it to multiple target languages, and showcase its capability to effortlessly learn multiple target languages while achieving superior results in zero-shot translation tasks. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks. It uses bidirectional propagation and alignment to exploit information in video sequences. In our research, we introduce an improved BasicVSR model, called ImprovedVSR, by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a novel deformable alignment guided by optical flow within convolutional layers. These enhancements enhance BasicVSR's ability to extract relevant information from video sequences, thereby improving its performance. Experimental results demonstrate that ImprovedVSR surpasses state-of-the-art video super-resolution models, with our method even achieving better results when employed as pre-training for other tasks, such as video restoration and object detection. We also provide insight into the benefits of using grid propagation and optical flow-guided alignment. Our source code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub. https://github.com/ExcitedHui/ImprovedVSR.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a model when it's trained on a variety of related tasks.  While
existing methods typically train across all tasks at once, leading to optimal
results, they often result in complex controllers that struggle with each task.
  By instead using a structured learning approach across multiple tasks, we
propose Q-learning for a specific order of tasks to take advantage of previously
acquired skills in each new task, resulting in better performance and reduced
complexity.  We test our method, Structured Multi-task Q-learning (SMLQ), in
a grid-world navigation scenario with a significant difference in goal positions
and sizes, finding it results in a significant reduction in controller complexity
while still surpassing the performance of traditional multi-task Q-learning.  We
also observe SMLQ's ability to handle varied task configurations and find it
outperforms alternative methods in these scenarios.  Overall, our method shows
great potential in real-world situations (e.g. in self-driving cars), particularly
when there are significant variations in goal positions and sizes.  As a result,
our approach results in reduced controller complexity, making it more in line with
current deep reinforcement learning systems.  As such, we examine the applicability
of SMLQ to deep reinforcement learning, finding it can be implemented in this manner
with deep neural networks, leading to improved performance and reduced controller
simplicity.  As such, our method provides a bridge between the existing literature
on multi-task reinforcement learning and the more practical deep reinforcement learning
systems used in current applications.  Ultimately, our results indicate a more
efficient pathway to multi-task reinforcement learning systems that are both more

We have improved the performance of minimum-work and maximum-efficiency protocols in finite-time stochastic heat engines by implementing adaptive adjustments to temperature and scaling parameters based on real-time feedback from the system and heat bath. The new optimized protocols exhibit exceptional robustness in their effectiveness, remaining nearly optimal under various conditions of limited knowledge, including situations where the scaling parameter is essentially unbounded. The freedom to adjust temperatures and parameters allows us to develop maximum-efficiency protocols that can be classified into two categories - passive and active strategies. While the passive strategies show a clear connection with the reversible path, the active approaches demonstrate a more complex relationship, but both categories share the characteristic of not being continuous in the temperature. However, we have discovered a specific condition under which the active strategies can be continuously linked to the reversible path, achieving a key standard in efficiency known as the Curzon-Fenstermak limit. Furthermore, we have found that the maximum-efficiency protocols can be classified into two types - one of which is passive, where the heat-to-work conversion ratio becomes independent of the temperature scaling parameter, while the other is active, resulting in a ratio dependent on the average scaling parameter. The new maximum-efficiency protocols have been proven to remain effective even under constraints of limited knowledge, while also showing exceptional performance in the particular case of unbounded scaling parameters. The exceptional performance of these new protocols has been confirmed through numerical implementation in the linear model, demonstrating their potential to outperform current engines by up to 300% in average work output. The outstanding features of these new protocols make them extremely valuable, as they can be easily applied to a wide variety of stochastic heat engines working within different thermal cycles. This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that power system load can be significantly reduced in areas affected by hurricane storms, and these outcomes vary significantly depending on the specific hurricane scenario, with some substations experiencing greater damage than others as the hurricane moves over the region. These findings are valued at approximately $1 billion, $3 billion, and $4 billion for three different hurricane scenarios, and these estimates suggest that storm-related power outages can result in substantial economic losses. Additionally, the study reveals that power system load may drop by as much as 50% in areas affected by hurricane storms, and these outcomes persist for an extended period after the initial storm passage. Notably, the proposed model can be applied to other critical infrastructure systems such as water and gas treatment plants, and similar analyses may be conducted for other regions utilizing the proposed approach. This framework is designed to facilitate probabilistic risk assessments and inform decision-makers on potential hazards. To implement the proposed model, the study employs open-source software such as OpenSees and PyGMT, and reveals the feasibility of combining probabilistic storm scenarios with actual meteorological and oceanographic data to simulate real-world hurricane scenarios. Finally, the proposed model can be applied to other regional power grids such as the Southeast and West Coast, and is versatile enough to be used in various engineering fields such as civil, mechanical, and electrical engineering. Some of the software used to implement the model is available online at \url{https://github.com/UT-EMRL/StormSurgeSimulator}. Additionally, the data employed in this study can be accessed at \url{https://utemrl.github.io/data-stormsurge/}. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. Additionally, we explore connections between the heterochaos baker map and complex systems, utilizing the generalized baker map as a tool for understanding unstable dimension variability and its relation to the Mandelbrot set. As future research objectives, we mention applications related to decoding chaotic signals and modeling brain function. Ultimately, we establish that the heterochaos baker map serves as a precise model for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. (The detailed paper is an expansion of our 2021 presentation at ICM 2022.)\par In the study of complex systems, it has been observed that certain properties of dynamic models appear across various fields including biology, physics, and mathematics. This report summarizes the primary findings from ATLAS and CMS experiments regarding the properties of the Higgs boson, its production modes, and searches for additional scalar particles. A notable focus is on the theoretical models proposed to explain the naturally low energy scale of the Higgs particle within the context of supersymmetry, specifically focusing on the production of scalar particles with complex couplings, including the direct detection of dark matter candidates. In addition, this document delves into more specialized topics such as the measurement of the Higgs boson's CP properties, its parabolic decay mode, and the search for the lightest supersymmetric particle. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior information in speech makes the model prone to pitch errors. We address this issue in speech synthesis by incorporating a pitch-dependent neural network. Specifically, the PCC-based optimization technique is used to adapt WN's weights to the speaker-dependent level. We also propose an optimization method to refine the model parameters in low pitch conditions. Notably, the PCC-based technique significantly improves the model's accuracy in high pitch ranges. Furthermore, the refinement method shortens WN training time without sacrificing its performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms WN and its extended versions, and matches the performance of the Model 5 in Tacotron2. We also observed that using PCC-based optimization often leads to smaller model sizes without affecting the speech quality. Our method's flexibility allows it to be applied to pre-trained models, as in the case of the extended Model 5 in Tacotron2. Finally, the PCC-based optimization achieved a 62% reduction in WN's weights while maintaining its performance. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of E-commerce and our daily lives. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to over-satisfaction and satisfaction disparities. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel CF approach that leverages Graph Attention Networks (GAT) to focus on fairness in recommendations. By modeling user and item similarities with adaptive node and edge embeddings, this GAT-based CF enhances interaction fairness compared to state-of-the-art CF and deep learning methods, as validated by experiments on real-world datasets. Additionally, our proposed approach exhibits long-term generalization capabilities similar to its static counterpart. Notably, this research is one of the few initiatives to apply GAT in Recommender Systems through a comprehensive empirical analysis. In particular, our study seeks to answer three crucial questions: (1) Can GAT-enhanced CF outperform other CF and deep learning-based methods in interaction fairness? (2) How does CF architecture with GAT node and edge attention enhance interaction fairness? (3) What is the effect of attention on performance compared to non-selective attention approaches? The findings of this research confirm the superiority of GAT-enhanced CF over other methods in achieving interaction fairness, demonstrating the effectiveness of CF architecture with GAT node and edge attention, and showing the fairness disparity between selective and non-selective attention approaches. Based on these results, our proposed approach serves as a potential solution to address fairness in Recommender Systems effectively. In future research, we aim to extend this work using side information to address additional challenges in Recommender Systems. In addition, we will apply this research to address various forms of bias in Recommender Systems, such as bias related to gender, age, and price. Ultimately, we hope to develop a Recommender System that can provide fair and fairable recommendations to users. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the Sun's surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Like the 'H$\alpha$ enhancement' and 'Ca II K core shift', our indicator exhibited a positive correlation with the solar faculae area, although the 'SII 6370 Angstroms line shift' was found to be unrelated to this activity measure. When evaluated using the HARPS-N data, these indicators displayed equivalent sensitivity to a star's activity level, all roughly mirroring a star's vacuum $S_{6370}$ index in proportion to $\lambda$ (from 3900 to 4200 Angstroms), although the indicators may be more suitable for specific observations, as observed in this research. When tested in a fake planetary signal, these novel indicators were found to outperform traditional activity indicators in a real-world dataset. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a compact, interpretable vector known as a style patch. By representing a style patch as a activation pattern within a pre-trained deep neural network's final convolutional layer, our method succeeds in accurately replicating the desired stylistic information across an input image. Furthermore, our style patches enable the achievement of multiple different publication-style results for a single input image, thereby retaining consistency with the original data. Unlike other neural network-based style transfer methods, our approach is notable for its minimalism due to its use of the pre-trained model, reducing the need for substantial computational resources or extensive training time. Additionally, our style patches can be freely downloaded from our website, providing a means of freely sharing the various style-specific information we have obtained. Ultimately, our research seeks to demonstrate that style-specific information can be effectively captured through a straightforward, easy-to-understand process, thereby providing a more versatile and efficient alternative to existing deep learning-based methods. Our style patches are available at https://vision.cs.washington.edu/stylepatch for download. Additionally, our code is available at https://github.com/alexalex27/style-patches for use. Lastly, our video showcasing our method's capabilities is available at https://vision.cs.washington.edu/stylepatch/video.html for viewing. Our research was supported through funding from the National Science Foundation. \hr

Additionally, the reported results highlight the benefits of pre-trained backbones and methods incorporating multiple features. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's potential, its practical application is hindered by the high computational demands of Bayesian inference. To overcome this challenge, machine learning techniques have been used to develop simplified models that approximate the mental framework, and have shown positive outcomes in robot navigation. However, these studies were conducted using unsupervised learning methods that optimize a predefined objective function without considering the actual physical environment. Contrasting these approaches, this paper proposes a novel active inference framework based on supervised learning techniques that incorporates real-time feedback from the physical environment to fine-tune its objectives. The framework's efficacy was evaluated in a simulated study, and the results demonstrate its ability to navigate a complex scenario more effectively than systems using traditional objective functions. The success of this framework suggests a new research direction, and paves the way for its potential application in real-world settings. A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be 14% longer than the Pacific Lamprey's, making this innovative design a promising approach for robots navigating steep surfaces with limited support points. Additionally, the correlation observed between actuation and robot motion remains consistent across various climbing speeds and inclines, showcasing the potential for optimized control through machine learning techniques. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the deployment of robots like Trident in challenging environments that current robots cannot access. A comprehensive video demonstration is available at https://youtu.be/7VimD4mMzKw. All experimental data have been uploaded to https://doi.org/10.6082/m1kwf544 for public access. A manufacturer-independent design of the robot is currently being prepared for publication in a separate article. Until then, a basic design description, along with code and experimental data, can be found at https://git.io/SLNTRND. All materials are available to researchers at no cost. As the primary contributor to this project, I can be reached at [jian.xu@utexas.edu](jian.xu@utexas.edu) regarding any inquiries related to the study.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework. An added complexity of the immunotherapy costs is explored, showing the potential for the optimal treatment combination to vary depending on whether the costs are directly or indirectly associated with the cancer cell population. This research contributes to the development of practical probabilistic strategies for identifying optimal cancer treatment combinations. Further research will be directed at developing closed-loop control strategies, as well as applying this framework to more complex types of cancer. A potential extension of this work is presented in the supplementary material.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation. Leveraging these findings, we have proven that weak solutions to a modified version of the Euler equations, accounting for collisions with solid surfaces, preserve helicity. Furthermore, these results were applied to demonstrate that weak solutions to the biharmonic Euler equations and the 3D Rotating Euler equations also conserve helicity. Lastly, while studying these equations, we discovered a new result regarding the conservation of a mathematical quantity related to the product of velocity and vorticity. This result is notable as it is the first to address this property in a weak solution context. This work extends and combines previously existing methods while introducing novel approaches to achieve these findings. Ultimately, the conclusions presented in this research are based on a mathematical space that is associated with a specific time of integration. For example, if a flow is smooth, it is shown to conserve helicity over time; on the other hand, if a flow is weak but non-smooth, it is shown to conserve helicity on an average basis given sufficient time. This research presents a comprehensive addition to the existing literature on fluid dynamics. Specifically, the findings presented in sections 1.2, 1.4, and 1.5 are significant as they expand upon existing conservation principles, including the helicity of fluids without viscosity as discussed in reference [25], the helicity of barotropic fluids in reference [10], and the enstrophy of incompressible Euler equations in reference [16]. This research also extends existing methods in a conservative approach to the rotating Euler equations in a compact domain as discussed in reference [41] and develops novel ideas for the conservative closure of the Euler equation with a collision response function as presented in reference [40]. The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the far-field behavior. They demonstrated that the solutions found can be expressed as a sum of two components, one of which decays rapidly and is singular in the phase, while the other behaves similarly to the fundamental solution of the associated Schrödinger equation. Using this structure, they were able to derive a relationship, referred to as the reflection coefficient, r, that describes how energy is reflected at singular points and, in the process, established that the system's solutions depend solely on the properties of the initial phase. Consequently, they were able to show that the system's solutions are entirely defined by a set of ordinary differential equations under certain conditions. Notably, when the amplitude of the initial phase is small enough, the system's solutions exhibit helical wave propagation patterns. Furthermore, in the presence of multiple singular points, the system's solutions display periodic, wave-like behavior as time progresses. In addition to these findings, the researchers were able to demonstrate that, in scenarios where a singular point becomes disconnected from the rest of the system, it develops its own independent, oscillatory behavior over time. Finally, through numerical simulations, they were able to visualize various scenarios and validate their results, while also exploring other systems of equations with similar properties. These investigations have potential applications in the fields of electrical impedance tomography and scattering theory. Conversely, the problem's electrodynamical implications are yet to be fully understood. Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current systems. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called DyGED, which utilizes a generative model based on matrix factorization for transparent event detection in evolving networks.  Through extensive testing with various methods on different types of data, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternatives in accuracy, while also providing insight into network changes using low-rank matrices that represent event onsets.  To further evaluate DyGED, we conducted a theoretical analysis and found that it possesses asymptotic statistical guarantees for effective event identification.  Based on these findings, we confidently apply DyGED to real-world network data, including Twitter posts and red-green stock market predictions.  Overall, DyGED offers a reliable and interpretable event detection system for learning dynamic graphs.  Source code is available at https://github.com/yotoyt/DyGED. Characterizing colorectal polyps via histopathological analysis is crucial to assess their likelihood of becoming cancerous and to inform patient treatment decisions. Expert pathologists achieve high accuracy in this task through extensive training and experience, but their process is difficult to formalize and translate into computer-aided diagnosis systems. In this study, we develop a novel deep learning approach that leverages pairs of mismatched features from digitized slide images to detect suspicious areas indicative of malignancy. By focusing on polyp morphology rather than overall slide appearance, our method achieves 88% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve in distinguishing high-risk from low-risk adenomas. We attained this result without employing massive datasets, which is noteworthy. Additionally, our method enables the identification of areas prioritized for detailed examination by pathologists, thereby enhancing diagnostic efficiency. Overall, our technique is a significant step towards developing an intelligent diagnostic system that enhances pathologists' work and aids patient treatment decisions. Future work will focus on incorporating expert knowledge into the method to further boost its accuracy and clinical applicability. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to enhanced performance, evident in repeated circuit evaluations, leading to better energy levels in our experiments.  The open-source code for this process is available on GitHub at https://github.com/luca-aspella/QAOA_Bayes.  Moreover, our simulation outcomes are aligned with prior research, demonstrating the potential of this technique to translate to real-world applications in superconducting quantum computing systems.  Specifically, we achieved an approximate solution for a hard instance of the exact cover problem with an error rate of 4.95%, comparing favorably to a 9.16% error rate from a global optimizer.  We also successfully replicated the results of Babbage et al.'s study [2020] with an additional evaluation of the algorithm's average optimality and computational complexity, finding the former to be 81.2% and the latter to be 1.21$\times 10^4$, respectively.  Finally, we explored the algorithm's performance on more complex instances of the exact cover problem, finding that it was insensitive to circuit variations.  The potential of this technique to scale to larger problems and reduce the need for expensive quantum evaluations with fewer calls aligns with the goals of quantum computing, namely reduced classical computation and fewer Qubit evaluations for the same approximate solution quality.  Graduate students and researchers in computer science may find the attached code useful for further experimentation.  Our simulation outcomes also provide meaningful metrics for evaluating mixed quantum algorithms.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. By taking advantage of this invariance, we have developed a streamlined method for the practical calculation of asymptotic averages and correlation functions. This method also generalizes the existing approach to the average entropy production rate, while providing a unified framework for previous work. The application of our findings to specific models is detailed in a companion paper. The theoretical conclusions presented in this study are essential for the practical application of our methods to complex models and the ongoing analysis of their computational properties. The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from hydrodynamical models yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years. Ultimately, precise measurements of particle size are instrumental in deciding between different theoretical scenarios. If future studies confirm that the particle size significantly alters, as expected with changing dust levels, this exoplanet could serve as a model for a distinctive phase in planetary evolution. Conversely, inconclusive findings may indicate that the exoplanet could be an analogue for the "canary in the coal mine" warning of atmospheric loss in the early history of our solar system. In either case, this research could hold significant implications for exoplanetary exploration and the existing scientific understanding of planetary disintegration. Based on the current findings, it is suggested that the most effective strategy for observing this phase transition would be to concentrate on planets within a specific size range, situated around their host stars' inner boundary, as these planets would likely display peculiar patterns in transit. As a result, it is anticipated that a substantial discovery of exoplanets exhibiting similar characteristics is on the horizon. We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category. Additionally, we create a finite set of parameters for non-degenerate, weighted projective space holomorphic functions, allowing us to preserve the Milnor fibration across the entire space. This framework also enables us to derive parameter conditions for preserving the Milnor fibration in certain classes of holomorphic functions, including hypersurfaces and complete intersections. Furthermore, we calculate the specific boundaries of parameter sets for quadratic holomorphic functions and those defining hypersurfaces within the weighted projective space. Finally, based on distinct localization patterns, we categorize holomorphic functions of degree 10 that are non-degenerate, demonstrating that they exhibit a complex, geographically dispersed structure in function space. This research provides detailed mathematical modeling for this scenario. This work is also published under a slightly modified title as 'Algebro-geometric Milnor Fibration Analysis'. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by linear algebra capabilities such as matrix singular value decomposition, eigenvalue decomposition, and more. Additionally, Daany enhances the DataFrame by integrating Python-like capabilities like data grouping, pivot tables, and data merging. By incorporating data plotting through MatrixProfile, Daany expands its functionality to include time series analysis and forecasting capabilities. Further enhancements are planned to further expand Daany's features and functionality.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. Ultimately, it is suggested that history has inaccurately portrayed Galileo as a key scientific innovator, when in fact his true role was that of a teacher and popularizer of existing mathematical ideas. Key scientific contributions, such as the fundamental theorem of mechanics, were made by other individuals, including Kepler and Joseph-Louis Lagrange. It is also proposed that the scientific revolution was, in reality, a gradual process spanning centuries, as well as a response to the growing influence of mathematics on science, which is the primary topic of this chapter. Additional discussion is provided in Sabin (2012), as well as Sabin (2020), where this material is presented in detail. Further research is recommended in Sabin (2020), as well as Sabin (2021), to explore the subject in greater depth. Additionally, it is suggested that the scientific community should acknowledge that innovation is not always associated with originality, as scientific progress can result from gradual, systematic work. Finally, it is proposed that the legacy of the scientific revolution should be reevaluated, as science is not inherently opposed to philosophy, as it has often been portrayed. Conversely, it is suggested that the primary contribution of the scientific revolution, as well as the scientific community in general, is the integration of mathematical ideas into scientific work. This integration is not unique to the scientific community, as it is also characteristic of the broader scientific community, as will be discussed further in Sabin (2021). Additionally, it is suggested that the scientific community should strive to eliminate the perception of a dichotomy between science and philosophy, as it is detrimental to the scientific community. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to simulate a standard reconnection benchmark. By comparing kinetic and fluid models, we validate the MHD-AEPIC's ability to capture the varied scales of magnetic reconnection. Additionally, we examine the embedded PIC model's impact on the outcomes, including the interface between kinetic and fluid domains, as well as the computational costs associated with the embedded region. Our results indicate that the MHD-AEPIC model successfully replicates the characteristics of both kinetic and fluid models, yielding a thorough comprehension of the reconnection process across multiple scales. This study also demonstrates the efficacy of the MHD-AEPIC model in minimizing computational expenses while maintaining accuracy. As a result, the model presents a promising approach for tackling collisionless reconnection in realistic, complex configurations in the future.
